descriptors.title: Opportunity cost and scarcity
descriptors.description: why opportunity cost exists as decisions are made to allocate limited resources to meet unlimited needs and wants
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored influences on consumer choices and strategies for making informed personal consumer and financial choices (AC9HS6K08). They can identify that people make decisions about spending and saving but have not formally engaged with the economic concepts of scarcity, resource allocation, or opportunity cost.

nodes.label: Needs, wants and unlimited desire
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between needs and wants, and explain why human wants are effectively unlimited.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not distinguish needs from wants and grasp that wants are unlimited, the concept of scarcity and the resulting need for allocation choices will not make sense. Scarcity is only meaningful when unlimited wants collide with finite resources — students who blur needs and wants will treat resource limits as a solvable supply problem rather than a structural economic condition.
criteria: Identifies at least two needs and two wants, distinguishing them with a clear reason
Explains why human wants are unlimited, using a concrete personal or community example

width.minimum: Identify personal examples of needs and wants; explain that wants are unlimited and cannot all be satisfied.
width.typical: Distinguish needs from wants across personal, household and community contexts; explain the concept of unlimited wants using concrete local examples; identify that a community's combined wants always exceed available resources.
wider: Compare how needs and wants differ across cultural or socioeconomic contexts; for example, investigate how a remote First Nations community defines community needs versus wants and how these are prioritised
Examine how advertising and social influence expand perceived wants over time, using examples from contemporary media
Investigate how definitions of 'need' shift over time as societies develop; for example, whether internet access is now a need

modes.reason: Students often conflate needs and wants or assume that wants could eventually all be met with enough production. Invest in the reasoning scaffold: why unlimited wants are a permanent structural feature of economic life, not a temporary shortage problem.
Broader contexts — community, cultural, historical — reveal that unlimited wants are not a personal weakness but a universal economic condition, strengthening the conceptual foundation for scarcity.

nodes.label: Economic scarcity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain economic scarcity as the condition that results from unlimited wants meeting limited resources, and apply it to the three fundamental allocation questions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand wants as unlimited but fail to connect this to resource limits will not grasp why allocation decisions are structurally necessary. Without the scarcity concept, opportunity cost reads as merely a personal budgeting observation rather than an economic principle — the next node cannot build meaningfully.
criteria: Defines economic scarcity and distinguishes it from a temporary shortage
Applies at least one of the three allocation questions to a concrete resource example

width.minimum: Explain economic scarcity using one allocation context (what, how, or for whom to produce); give a concrete example of a scarce resource.
width.typical: Explain scarcity as the structural gap between unlimited wants and finite resources; apply to all three allocation questions (what, how, for whom); use examples from local community resource use including land, labour and capital.
wider: Investigate how First Nations communities use exchange systems (barter) or partnership networks to manage scarce resources sustainably across generations
Examine a contemporary resource scarcity case — such as water allocation in a drought-affected region — and analyse how the three allocation questions play out in practice
Explore how economic scarcity differs from physical scarcity: why something can be physically abundant but economically scarce (or vice versa)

modes.reason: The three allocation questions (what/how/for whom) are abstract for Year 7 students. Scaffold by working through a concrete local example — a school tuckshop, a community garden — and applying each question explicitly before generalising.

nodes.label: Opportunity cost
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of opportunity cost — what is given up when a choice is made — in relation to a specific allocation decision.
criteria: Defines opportunity cost accurately in own words
Identifies the specific alternative forgone in a given resource allocation example

width.minimum: Define opportunity cost; identify the trade-off in one personal or community resource decision (e.g. time, money, land).
width.typical: Explain opportunity cost as the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made; apply to personal time and money decisions and to community or business resource allocation decisions; explain that opportunity cost is not the price paid but the value of the best alternative not chosen.
wider: Analyse opportunity costs in government spending decisions; for example, if state funds are directed to roads rather than hospitals, what is the opportunity cost?
Investigate how opportunity cost applies to non-monetary resources such as time, environmental capacity or cultural land use
Compare how First Nations communities weigh opportunity costs when balancing economic development against environmental and cultural custodianship

modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of decision contexts — personal, household, community, government — to distinguish opportunity cost from merely 'what you didn't buy'. Each new context reinforces that opportunity cost is always a real alternative forgone, not an abstract calculation.

nodes.label: Allocation, sustainability and integration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why opportunity cost arises from the structural condition of scarcity, and apply this reasoning to how limited resources are (or could be) allocated more sustainably.
criteria: Explains the logical chain from scarcity to opportunity cost using a specific resource example
Identifies at least one sustainability implication of a resource allocation decision
Uses economic terms (scarcity, needs, wants, opportunity cost, allocation) accurately in explanation

width.minimum: Explain the chain: unlimited wants → scarcity → allocation decision → opportunity cost. Apply to one resource allocation scenario including a sustainability consideration.
width.typical: Explain the full logical chain connecting scarcity to opportunity cost across personal and community contexts; discuss how resource allocation decisions can affect sustainability; evaluate whether a given allocation is meeting needs and wants into the future.
wider: Investigate how First Nations resource management practices embody long-term opportunity cost reasoning — prioritising intergenerational sustainability over short-term wants
Analyse a local council or community decision about land or infrastructure allocation and map out the opportunity costs and sustainability implications
Explore how the concept of 'common pool resources' (shared resources like fisheries or groundwater) illustrates scarcity and collective allocation challenges

modes.reason: This node requires students to connect all prior building blocks into a coherent economic argument: scarcity forces allocation choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. The teaching focus is on students producing an integrated explanation, not just listing the components.

descriptors.title: Types of businesses
descriptors.description: the reasons businesses exist and how different types of businesses provide goods and services
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored consumer choices and how individuals make financial decisions (AC9HS6K08). They are familiar with the idea of goods and services from everyday life but have not formally analysed why businesses exist, the range of business structures, or the distinction between goods-producing and service-providing enterprises.

nodes.label: Why businesses exist
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify multiple reasons why businesses exist beyond profit, including employment, community service, and production of goods and services.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that businesses exist for multiple reasons — not profit alone — is foundational for correctly analysing different business types in the next node. Students who reduce all business existence to profit-seeking will misclassify cooperatives, not-for-profits and First Nations enterprises, blocking meaningful engagement with business diversity.
criteria: Lists at least two distinct reasons businesses exist, beyond profit
Identifies one goods-providing and one service-providing business with an explanation of what each provides

width.minimum: Identify two or more reasons why businesses exist, including profit and at least one non-profit reason; give a concrete local example.
width.typical: Explain why businesses exist across a range of purposes — profit, employment, providing goods and services, meeting community needs; distinguish between goods-producing and service-providing businesses using local examples including shopping centres, markets, online platforms and independent stores.
wider: Investigate a First Nations-owned business and examine its founding purposes, exploring how community, cultural and economic motivations intersect
Compare why a for-profit corporation, a not-for-profit organisation, and a cooperative exist, analysing how their purposes shape what they provide and how
Examine how remote community stores differ from urban retailers in purpose, supply constraints and community role

modes.reason: Local community examples — including First Nations businesses, cooperatives and community stores — resolve the profit-only misconception more effectively than abstract definitions, because they make visible the genuine diversity of business purposes.

nodes.label: Types of business structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the features of different business types — sole proprietorship, partnership, cooperative, corporation, franchise, not-for-profit — and explain how structure relates to how goods and services are provided.
criteria: Names and describes at least three different business types with a distinguishing feature for each
Matches a real example to each business type identified

width.minimum: Identify at least three business types with a key distinguishing feature for each; give a real-world example of each type identified.
width.typical: Identify and describe the key features of sole proprietorship, partnership, cooperative, corporation, franchise and not-for-profit organisation; explain how each structure shapes how goods and services are provided, owned and operated; use local and national examples for each type.
wider: Analyse a cooperative — such as a First Nations community-run corporation — comparing its ownership and decision-making structure with a corporation or franchise
Investigate how franchises operate as a model: explore the relationship between franchisor and franchisee and how this shapes what the business can and cannot do
Examine how digital platforms (e.g. online marketplaces) represent newer business distribution models that sit alongside or inside traditional structures

modes.reason: Students need concrete exemplars for each structure type before they can apply the categories reliably. Build a running class reference of real local businesses mapped to their structure type, adding examples progressively as new structures are introduced.

nodes.label: Business types, goods, services and integration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how different types of businesses provide goods and services, connecting business structure and purpose to what is produced, how it reaches consumers, and why this matters.
criteria: Explains how at least two different business types provide goods or services differently, connecting structure to provision
Uses business terms (sole proprietor, corporation, cooperative, goods, services, franchise, not-for-profit) accurately in explanation

width.minimum: Explain how one business type provides goods or services, connecting its structure to what it produces and how it reaches consumers.
width.typical: Explain how a range of business types provide goods and services across different distribution channels (shopping centres, markets, online, independent stores, remote community stores); analyse how business structure and purpose shape what is provided and to whom.
wider: Compare how a First Nations-owned business and a major corporation provide similar goods or services — examining differences in supply chain, ownership, community benefit and cultural purpose
Evaluate how the shift to online business has changed the types of goods and services available and which business structures benefit most from digital distribution
Investigate a social enterprise: how does its structure enable it to pursue a community mission while still operating commercially?

modes.reason: This node coordinates the two prior building blocks — purposes and structures — into a complete explanation of how business type shapes what is provided and how. Students should be able to reason from structure to provision, not just label the type.

descriptors.title: Entrepreneurial characteristics
descriptors.description: characteristics of entrepreneurs and how these influence the success of a business
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand why businesses exist and can identify different business types (AC9HE7K02). They are building a picture of the business landscape but have not yet examined the human factors — knowledge, skills, values and attitudes — that drive business creation and success.

nodes.label: Entrepreneurial knowledge and skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the knowledge and skills entrepreneurs use, including opportunity recognition, decision-making and establishing a shared vision.
criteria: Identifies at least two entrepreneurial knowledge or skill areas
Provides a concrete example of each from a real entrepreneur

width.minimum: Identify two or more entrepreneurial knowledge or skill areas with a concrete example from a real entrepreneur or business story.
width.typical: Describe the entrepreneurial knowledge and skills that contribute to business creation and operation — recognising opportunities, establishing a shared vision, making decisions about business operations; use examples from local, national and First Nations Australian entrepreneurs.
wider: Research the entrepreneurial story of a First Nations Australian entrepreneur (e.g. Dean Foley, Tahnee Edwards, or a community-run company such as Gumatj Aboriginal Corporation) and map their entrepreneurial knowledge and skills to their business outcomes
Compare the knowledge and skill profile of an entrepreneur in a large corporation versus a sole proprietor in a local community, identifying similarities and differences
Investigate how digital skills have become part of contemporary entrepreneurial knowledge — examining how an online business was built by recognising a digital opportunity

modes.reason: Entrepreneurial knowledge and skills are abstract without a range of concrete exemplars. Build a running class set of entrepreneur profiles — local, national, and First Nations — from which students can identify and compare these knowledge and skill areas.

nodes.label: Values and entrepreneurial decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how values — including identifying opportunities, stakeholder negotiation, and compliance — influence entrepreneurial decision-making.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that values shape entrepreneurial decisions is necessary for the integration node, which requires students to explain how characteristics influence business success. Students who focus only on skills without considering values will produce incomplete explanations of entrepreneurial success and failure.
criteria: Identifies a specific value held by an entrepreneur and explains how it shaped a business decision
Connects the decision to an outcome for the business or community

width.minimum: Identify one example of how a personal or cultural value has influenced an entrepreneur's decision; explain the decision and its consequence.
width.typical: Analyse how values influence entrepreneurial decision-making across three areas: identifying and taking advantage of opportunities, negotiating with stakeholders, and complying with laws and regulations; apply to at least one specific entrepreneur with concrete evidence.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australian entrepreneurs navigate the intersection of business values and cultural responsibilities — using the Gumatj Aboriginal Corporation or a similar example to explore decision-making that balances economic and community obligations
Investigate a case where an entrepreneur's values led to a decision that prioritised community or environmental benefit over maximum profit, and evaluate the business outcome
Analyse a business decision that involved legal or regulatory compliance — what values drove compliance or non-compliance, and what were the consequences?

modes.reason: Students often treat values as personal opinions rather than as active factors in business decision-making. Scaffold with specific decision examples where the value is identifiable and traceable to an outcome: 'This entrepreneur valued community employment, so they chose X over Y, resulting in Z.'

First Nations entrepreneurial contexts offer particularly rich value-decision cases — where cultural, community and economic values intersect — and help students move beyond a profit-centric model of entrepreneurial motivation.

nodes.label: Characteristics and business success
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine entrepreneurial knowledge, skills and attitudes with observations of businesses to explain the factors that contribute to success, including opportunity recognition, initiative and innovation.
criteria: Explains how at least two specific entrepreneurial characteristics contributed to a business's success
Uses evidence from the business's story to support the explanation
Uses relevant terms (entrepreneur, opportunity, initiative, innovation, stakeholder) accurately

width.minimum: Explain how at least two entrepreneurial characteristics contributed to the success of a specific business; use evidence from the business's story.
width.typical: Combine knowledge, skills and attitudes demonstrated by entrepreneurs with observations of successful local businesses to explain factors contributing to success, including opportunity recognition, initiative and innovation; apply to at least two entrepreneurs from different business or cultural contexts.
wider: Compare how entrepreneurial success is defined differently across cultural contexts — for example, contrasting a First Nations entrepreneur whose success is measured by community benefit with a corporate entrepreneur measured by financial return
Evaluate a failed business venture and identify which entrepreneurial characteristics were absent or underdeveloped, explaining how this contributed to the outcome
Research a local or regional business and develop an original framework for what characteristics contributed most to its success, using evidence from public sources

modes.reason: The final node integrates skills, values and attitudes into a cohesive explanation of business success. Students need to move beyond listing characteristics to constructing a causal argument: these characteristics, in this context, produced this outcome.

descriptors.title: Work, income and identity
descriptors.description: the reasons individuals work, the types of work they are involved in, and how they may derive an income
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored consumer choices and personal financial decision-making (AC9HS6K08). They have encountered the idea that people earn income but have not formally examined the full range of work types, income sources, or the social and identity dimensions of work — including unpaid, volunteer and First Nations community contributions.

nodes.label: Types of work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe different types of work — full-time, part-time, casual, at home, paid, unpaid, volunteer — and explain that not all work is formally recognised or remunerated.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise formal paid employment as 'work' will be unable to explain the full range of income sources in the next node, and will miss the social and identity contributions of work that are central to the descriptor's scope. The narrow view also prevents engagement with First Nations and community work contexts.
criteria: Names at least four distinct types of work with an example of each
Distinguishes between paid and unpaid work and explains why both contribute to individuals and communities

width.minimum: Identify at least four types of work with a concrete example of each; distinguish between paid and unpaid work.
width.typical: Identify and describe the full range of work types — full-time, part-time, casual, at home, paid, unpaid, unrecognised and volunteer; explain that unpaid and volunteer work contributes to community even when not formally recognised; use examples from students' own communities.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' management of Country/Place constitutes a form of work — including cultural maintenance, land management and knowledge transmission — that may not be captured in formal employment data
Examine how unpaid domestic work is distributed and valued differently across households, and discuss whether it should be counted in national economic measures
Explore how volunteer work sustains community organisations and services — interview a local volunteer or examine a community organisation's reliance on non-paid contributions

modes.reason: Expanding beyond wage work to include unpaid, volunteer and cultural custodianship work requires multiple concrete examples from different community contexts. Each new context adds a genuinely distinct category to students' understanding of what 'work' encompasses.

nodes.label: How individuals derive an income
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the different ways people derive an income, including wages, salaries, business ownership, dividends, rental income, and social security.
criteria: Identifies at least three different income sources with a concrete example for each
Explains the difference between at least two income sources (e.g. wage vs. business profit)

width.minimum: Identify at least three ways of deriving income with a concrete example for each; explain the difference between a wage and a salary.
width.typical: Describe the ways people derive income — working for a wage or salary, owning a business, being a shareholder (dividends), providing a rental service, receiving social security; explain how each income source relates to a different economic role.
wider: Investigate how a First Nations community enterprise generates income for its members and community — examining income streams that combine commercial revenue, grant funding and cultural services
Explore how passive income sources (rental, dividends) differ from active income in terms of economic effort and risk
Examine how gig economy work (e.g. delivery platforms, freelancing) creates income that is neither wage nor salary — and what this means for financial security

modes.reason: Students benefit from a growing set of concrete income-source examples before integrating them with work types. Build a class matrix pairing work types with income sources — e.g. volunteer work → no income; rental property owner → rental income.

nodes.label: Reasons for working: identity, community and wellbeing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the multiple reasons individuals work beyond earning income, including identity, self-esteem, community contribution and material and non-material living standards.
criteria: Explains at least two reasons individuals work beyond earning income
Uses relevant terms (identity, living standards, material, non-material, volunteer) accurately in explanation

width.minimum: Explain two reasons individuals work other than earning income, using a specific example for each.
width.typical: Analyse the contribution work makes to individuals' identity and community roles — including earning income, self-esteem, happiness, community support through volunteering, and material and non-material living standards; apply to a range of work contexts including paid, unpaid and culturally significant work.
wider: Examine how continuity of cultural practices and management of Country/Place contributes to and sustains First Nations communities — analysing how this work contributes to identity, wellbeing and economic sustainability through regional tourism ventures, mentoring and entrepreneurship
Investigate a case where a person chose lower-income work for personal or community reasons — exploring the trade-offs between material and non-material living standards
Analyse how the reasons people work have changed across generations, using evidence from older family members, community data or historical examples

modes.reason: Students default to income as the only reason people work. Scaffold explicitly: income is one reason; what else does work provide that money alone cannot? Work through identity, purpose, community belonging and cultural connection as distinct contributions.

First Nations community work — cultural maintenance, mentoring, land management — provides a particularly strong context for seeing non-income motivations as genuine and substantial, not supplementary.

descriptors.title: Consumer and financial rights and responsibilities
descriptors.description: the rights and responsibilities of individuals and businesses in relation to consumer and financial products and services
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored consumer choices and strategies for making informed financial decisions (AC9HS6K08) and are developing understanding of work and income (AC9HE7K04). They are familiar with making purchases but have not formally examined the legal and ethical framework of rights and responsibilities that governs consumer and financial transactions.

nodes.label: Rights versus responsibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between rights and responsibilities, and apply this distinction to consumer and financial contexts.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish rights from responsibilities at the conceptual level, they will not be able to correctly assign rights and responsibilities to parties in specific consumer scenarios in subsequent nodes. The distinction underpins all analysis of who is entitled to what and who is obligated to whom.
criteria: Defines rights and responsibilities in own words with a clear distinction
Gives one example of a consumer right and one consumer responsibility for an individual

width.minimum: Distinguish rights from responsibilities with a clear definition; give one consumer example of each.
width.typical: Distinguish rights (entitlements that can be claimed) from responsibilities (obligations that must be met) in everyday language; develop a list of rights and responsibilities for both individuals and businesses in consumer and financial contexts.
wider: Examine how consumer rights vary across different contexts — for example, purchasing from a large corporation versus a local market stallholder, or buying online versus in-store
Explore how the concept of rights and responsibilities was codified in Australian consumer law — what prompted the development of formal consumer protections?
Investigate how consumer rights differ for First Nations communities in remote areas accessing goods through community stores, and what responsibilities fall on those store operators

modes.reason: Students often conflate rights and responsibilities or use them interchangeably. Scaffold with a clear definitional contrast — a right is something you can claim; a responsibility is something you must fulfil — then apply to concrete examples where the parties are identifiable.

nodes.label: Individual rights in consumer and financial contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the rights of individuals in relation to consumer and financial products and services, including warranties, cooling-off periods and return processes.
criteria: Explains at least two individual consumer rights with a concrete example of each
Describes what a warranty or cooling-off period is and when it applies

width.minimum: Explain two individual consumer rights — such as the right to a warranty or a cooling-off period — with a concrete example of how each applies.
width.typical: Explain the rights of individuals in relation to consumer and financial products and services including: warranties, cooling-off periods, and processes for returning goods; apply each right to a realistic consumer scenario.
wider: Investigate the Australian Consumer Law and identify at least three consumer rights it codifies — examining how the law translates abstract rights into enforceable protections
Explore how digital purchases (apps, subscriptions, online goods) create consumer rights questions that differ from traditional in-store purchases
Examine how consumers can exercise their rights in practice — who to contact, what to say, and what documentation to keep — developing a practical guide for a Year 7 audience

modes.reason: Students need concrete exposure to specific rights before they can reason about how rights and responsibilities balance. Build a set of scenario cards — each presenting a consumer situation — and have students identify which right applies and how to exercise it.

nodes.label: Business responsibilities and product safety
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the responsibilities of businesses in relation to consumer and financial products and services, including mandatory and voluntary standards and product safety recalls.
criteria: Explains at least two business responsibilities with a real example of each
Describes what a product safety recall is and what the business is responsible for doing

width.minimum: Identify two business responsibilities in consumer or financial contexts with a concrete example; explain what happens when a business fails to meet these responsibilities.
width.typical: Explain business responsibilities in consumer and financial contexts including: mandatory and voluntary standards, product safety recalls, and obligations to provide accurate information; apply to real-world examples of businesses meeting or failing their responsibilities.
wider: Analyse a real product safety recall — what triggered it, what the business was responsible for doing, and what the consequences were for consumers and the business
Compare mandatory versus voluntary standards: why would a business voluntarily adopt standards beyond legal requirements? What incentives exist?
Investigate the responsibilities of a financial services business (such as a bank) toward its customers — exploring how these differ from general product responsibilities

modes.reason: Product recalls, financial services responsibilities and voluntary standards are sufficiently different in mechanism and consequence that separate concrete examples are needed for each. Students who only see one context will not be able to explain the range of business responsibilities.

nodes.label: Budgeting, decision-making and integration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how developing personal or business budgets and savings plans supports better decision-making about consumer and financial products and services, integrating rights and responsibilities into that framework.
criteria: Explains why a budget or savings plan supports better consumer or financial decisions
Connects the budgeting rationale to at least one consumer right or business responsibility
Uses relevant terms (rights, responsibilities, warranty, budget, standards, product safety) accurately

width.minimum: Explain why a budget or savings plan is useful before making a consumer or financial decision; link this to one right or responsibility identified in prior nodes.
width.typical: Explain the importance of budgets and savings plans for individuals and businesses as a foundation for informed consumer and financial decisions; connect budgeting to exercising consumer rights responsibly (e.g. not over-committing, understanding what you've agreed to); apply to a realistic decision scenario.
wider: Develop a simple personal budget for a hypothetical consumer decision and map the rights and responsibilities that apply at each stage of the purchase

Examine how access to budgeting and financial literacy tools differs across communities — including remote and First Nations communities — and what this means for exercising consumer rights effectively
Investigate how businesses use budgets and financial planning to meet their responsibilities to consumers — for example, setting aside funds for warranty claims or recalls

modes.reason: This node coordinates rights, responsibilities and financial decision-making into a coherent whole. Students should be able to reason: informed decision-making depends on both knowing your rights and planning your finances — these reinforce each other.

descriptors.title: Develop inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed questions about people, events, developments, places and systems in primary HASS (AC9HS6S01). They can form basic inquiry questions but have not yet applied economic and business concepts and vocabulary systematically to question construction, nor targeted their questions specifically at contemporary issues.

nodes.label: What makes a question investigable
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between open, investigable questions and closed or unanswerable questions in an economic and business context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions will produce driving questions that cannot be meaningfully answered with data or evidence — the entire investigation phase collapses if the question is circular, too narrow, or unanswerable.
criteria: Identifies a question as investigable or not-investigable and gives a reason
Explains at least two features of a good investigable question

width.minimum: Identify one investigable and one non-investigable question about an economic topic; explain the difference.
width.typical: Distinguish between closed, leading and open investigable questions in economics and business; explain what makes a question useful as the basis for an investigation (e.g. answerable using data/evidence, economically relevant, contemporary); apply to provided examples.
wider: Examine why the same economic situation (e.g. rising prices, a new business opening) can generate multiple different investigable questions depending on the investigator's perspective or purpose
Analyse a sample student investigation and evaluate whether its driving question was investigable — and what a better question might have been

modes.reason: The distinction between a question and an investigable question is not obvious at Year 7. Scaffold by working through examples: 'Is scarcity real?' is not investigable; 'How does our school allocate its limited resources to meet student needs?' is. Students need to see and evaluate the contrast before generating their own.

nodes.label: Using economics concepts in question construction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions using economic and business concepts and terms such as scarcity, opportunity cost, market, income, goods and services.
criteria: Develops at least one investigable question that correctly uses an economics or business concept
The question is answerable using accessible data or sources

width.minimum: Develop one question using at least one economic or business concept correctly; the question must be investigable.
width.typical: Develop questions using a range of economic and business concepts and terms — scarcity, opportunity cost, market, income, business, goods and services, costs and benefits — framed as investigable questions about contemporary issues; refine questions to ensure they are answerable using accessible data or sources.
wider: Develop a set of linked sub-questions that unpack a complex economic issue — practising how a main investigation question can be broken into component investigable questions
Peer-review a partner's question set using an explicit criterion checklist for economic vocabulary, investigability and contemporary relevance
Develop questions specifically about a First Nations economic context (e.g. 'How does the Gumatj Corporation decide how to allocate its resources?') and evaluate their investigability

modes.reason: Students need practice generating and revising questions across multiple economic topics before the skill becomes transferable. Provide question stems that prompt concept use ('How does... affect...?', 'What is the opportunity cost of...?') and have students adapt them to different issues.

descriptors.title: Locate and organise information
descriptors.description: locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate, collect and organise information from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats (AC9HS6S02). At Year 7, the demand shifts to selecting from a wider range of source types — including government and NGO websites and digital tools — and to organising using more specialised formats such as tables, graphs and visual displays.

nodes.label: Locating sources using targeted search
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate relevant economics and business sources using targeted search techniques, including advanced search functions.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot locate sources reliably using targeted search, their entire information base will be too broad, biased or unreliable to support a meaningful investigation. Weak locating cascades through selection and organisation phases.
criteria: Locates at least two relevant sources for an economic topic
Describes the search terms or strategy used and explains why they were chosen

width.minimum: Locate two relevant sources for an economic topic using a search engine; describe the search terms used.
width.typical: Locate online sources using targeted search techniques — advanced search functions ('define: market'), targeted criteria ('allintext: successful Australian entrepreneurs'), government department and NGO websites; explain how the search approach was tailored to the question.
wider: Compare the results of a broad versus a targeted search for the same economic topic — evaluating which approach yields more relevant, reliable sources
Collaborate with a peer to exchange information online with an entrepreneur or industry contact to gather primary source data
Explore how to locate First Nations economic and business sources — including community organisations, AIATSIS and First Nations business directories — and evaluate their reliability and relevance

modes.reason: Targeted search is a precision skill that degrades when students default to broad keyword searches. Targeted practice with economics-specific search techniques — including 'define:' and 'allintext:' operators — builds reliable searching habits that carry through the investigation.

nodes.label: Selecting relevant information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select information and data from sources by evaluating its relevance to their investigation question.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish relevant from irrelevant information will collect indiscriminately, producing disorganised and unfocused responses. The selection criterion — 'does this help answer my question?' — is the discipline that makes subsequent organisation and interpretation meaningful.
criteria: Selects at least two pieces of information from a source with a stated reason for relevance
Discards or sets aside information identified as not relevant to the investigation question

width.minimum: Select two pieces of information from a source and explain how each helps answer the investigation question.
width.typical: Select relevant information and data from a range of sources by applying the question 'How will this data or information help answer my question?'; distinguish relevant from irrelevant information; apply to websites of government departments and non-government organisations.
wider: Evaluate conflicting information from two sources on the same economic issue — explaining which is more useful and why
Practise selective use of a complex multi-variable dataset: identify only the variables needed to answer a specific question and exclude the rest
Evaluate the relevance and reliability of information provided by an entrepreneur contacted online, and identify what follow-up questions would strengthen the data

modes.reason: Students need a practical decision rule they can apply at source level: for each piece of information, ask 'Does this directly help answer my question?' Scaffold this as a routine check, not a post-hoc judgement.

nodes.label: Organising data using appropriate formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise information and data into appropriate formats — tables, graphs, visual displays — using digital tools.
criteria: Organises selected information into an appropriate format using a digital tool
Explains why the chosen format suits the data type

width.minimum: Organise selected information into one appropriate format (table or graph) using a digital tool; explain why the format suits the data.
width.typical: Organise data into appropriate formats using specialised digital tools — tables, graphs, visual displays; select the format that best suits the type and purpose of the data; apply to economics data (e.g. income data, business type counts, consumer trend data).
wider: Organise multi-variable data (e.g. employment type by age group) into a format that makes the relevant relationship visible — comparing multiple format options before selecting
Curate a visual display combining data from multiple sources — practising how to integrate information from different formats into a coherent organised product
Use a digital tool to organise qualitative data (e.g. interview responses from an entrepreneur) into a structured format suitable for analysis

modes.reason: Format selection requires practice with real data across multiple types. Students who default to one format (usually a table) need explicit experience with graphs and visual displays to build a repertoire of organisation strategies.

descriptors.title: Interpret information and data
descriptors.description: interpret information and data to identify economic and business issues, trends and economic cause-and-effect relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate information and data to identify and describe patterns and trends, and infer relationships (AC9HS6S03). The Year 7 demand adds specific economic frames — identifying issues, identifying multi-variable trends using interactive digital tools, and reasoning about cause-and-effect relationships in economic contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying economic issues from information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret information to identify an economic or business issue, making an inference beyond what is directly stated.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can only describe what data shows — without inferring the issue behind it — will not be able to engage with trend identification or cause-and-effect reasoning in subsequent nodes. Interpretation that stops at 'what happened' cannot advance to 'what issue does this reveal or what caused it.'
criteria: Identifies an economic or business issue from provided information
Explains the inference made — what in the information pointed to the issue

width.minimum: Interpret one piece of economic information and identify the issue it points to; explain the inference made.
width.typical: Interpret information from a range of sources to identify economic and business issues; make inferences beyond the data — for example, inferring the effect of growth in online shopping on the number of customers entering physical stores.
wider: Interpret multiple pieces of information about the same economic issue from sources with different perspectives (e.g. business data vs consumer survey) and explain how each reveals a different aspect of the issue
Identify an economic issue affecting a First Nations community by interpreting community economic data or a published community report
Examine a news article or data release and identify two distinct economic issues it raises — practising the separation of connected issues

modes.reason: Students need an explicit inference scaffold: 'The data shows X. This suggests Y is happening. The economic issue this points to is Z.' Practise the move from data observation to issue identification before asking students to do it independently.

nodes.label: Identifying trends using multi-variable data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret multi-variable data using interactive digital tools to identify trends and answer specific questions about economic change over time.
criteria: Identifies and describes a trend in a multi-variable dataset using a digital tool
Answers a directed question about the trend using evidence from the data

width.minimum: Use a provided digital tool to identify one trend in a two-variable economic dataset; describe the trend in economic terms.
width.typical: Interpret multi-variable data using interactive digital tools — identifying trends, answering directed questions such as 'For a 10-year period, how has the number of people in casual work changed?'; explain what the trend reveals about the economic context.
wider: Compare trends across two different time periods or demographic groups in the same dataset — identifying whether a trend is consistent or variable
Select an appropriate digital tool to investigate a self-directed trend question about a contemporary economic issue, justifying the tool and dataset choice
Interpret employment trend data disaggregated by gender or regional area and identify what this reveals about differential economic participation

modes.reason: Students need experience with multiple dataset types and digital tools before they can apply trend identification independently. Build fluency through a sequence of increasingly complex datasets — starting with simple two-variable line graphs, progressing to multi-variable interactive displays.

nodes.label: Cause-and-effect relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret visual displays of multi-variable data to identify a cause-and-effect relationship within an economic issue, such as the relationship between income and saving or spending behaviour.
criteria: Identifies a cause-and-effect relationship in a visual data display
Explains the direction of the relationship using evidence from the data
Uses economic terms (trend, cause, effect, relationship, variable) accurately

width.minimum: Identify one cause-and-effect relationship in a visual display of economic data; explain which variable is the cause and which is the effect.
width.typical: Interpret visual displays of multi-variable data to identify cause-and-effect relationships — for example, the relationship between income and levels of saving and spending; explain the direction and nature of the relationship using evidence from the data; distinguish correlation from causation.
wider: Analyse a case where an apparent economic cause-and-effect relationship is complicated by a third variable — practising the distinction between correlation and causation
Investigate a cause-and-effect relationship in the context of a First Nations community economic issue — for example, how access to financial services affects saving behaviour in remote communities
Compare cause-and-effect relationships in consumer behaviour data across different demographic groups, identifying what additional variables might explain differences

modes.reason: Cause-and-effect reasoning in economics requires students to hold the relationship structure in mind: 'X changes, which causes Y to change, because...' The 'because' is the economic reasoning. Students need scaffolded practice constructing the full chain, not just labelling the correlation.

descriptors.title: Develop a response to an economic issue
descriptors.description: develop a response to an economic and business issue, identifying potential costs and benefits
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop evidence-based conclusions and propose actions with assessed effects (AC9HS6S05, AC9HS6S06). The Year 7 demand adds the economic frame of costs and benefits — structuring a response to an issue by explicitly identifying and weighing the trade-offs involved, and explaining that a decision selects one alternative over another.

nodes.label: What counts as a cost and a benefit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the potential costs and benefits of an economic decision, recognising that both financial and non-financial factors count.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce costs and benefits to financial amounts only will be unable to construct a complete response to an economic issue. Non-financial costs and benefits — time, social impact, opportunity cost, environmental effects — are essential to the full economic analysis demanded by the descriptor and the integration node.
criteria: Identifies at least one financial and one non-financial cost and benefit for a given decision
Explains why each factor counts as a cost or benefit

width.minimum: Identify at least one cost and one benefit for a given decision; include at least one non-financial factor.
width.typical: Identify the potential costs and benefits of an economic decision — including both financial and non-financial factors such as time, opportunity cost, social impact; distinguish direct from indirect costs and benefits; apply to realistic consumer and community decisions.
wider: Analyse costs and benefits in a government resource allocation decision — where community benefit may be broad and indirect, and costs distributed unevenly across groups
Examine how a First Nations community might assess the costs and benefits of a new economic development proposal — weighing financial returns against cultural, environmental and community impacts
Evaluate a historical business decision by identifying costs and benefits at the time versus in retrospect — exploring how uncertainty affects cost-benefit analysis

modes.reason: The cost-benefit scaffold needs to be explicit: costs = what you give up (money, time, other options); benefits = what you gain (money, time, satisfaction, community good). Students need the non-financial categories named and modelled before applying independently.

nodes.label: Reasoning from cost-benefit to a response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine known knowledge with new ideas to develop a response to an economic issue, using costs and benefits to justify the response.
criteria: Develops a response to an economic issue that identifies costs and benefits of the chosen option
Explains why one alternative was selected over another using cost-benefit reasoning

width.minimum: Develop a response to a structured issue — such as a purchase or part-time work decision — that uses identified costs and benefits as the reasoning basis.
width.typical: Develop a response to an issue by combining known knowledge with new ideas — for example, using a product statement and personal budget to identify benefits and costs of a mobile phone purchase; explain why making an economic decision involves selecting one alternative over another; use cost-benefit reasoning as the explicit justification structure.
wider: Develop a response to a community-level economic issue (e.g. 'Should the local council convert parkland to commercial development?') using a full cost-benefit analysis
Develop a response that explicitly addresses a sustainability dimension — identifying costs that accrue over time or benefits that are only realised in the long term
Develop a response to an economic issue facing a First Nations community, engaging with the specific costs and benefits as understood from within that community context

modes.reason: Students need practice constructing the full reasoning chain: 'The issue is X. The alternatives are A and B. The costs of A are... the benefits of A are... Therefore my response is A, because...' Without this scaffold, cost-benefit identification stays at listing rather than becoming the basis of a reasoned response.

descriptors.title: Create descriptions and explanations
descriptors.description: create descriptions and explanations, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present descriptions and explanations drawing on findings and viewpoints from sources using relevant terms and conventions (AC9HS6S07). The Year 7 demand adds domain-specific economic vocabulary — market, income, business, goods and services, costs and benefits — and requires students to embed data and information from sources explicitly in their explanations.

nodes.label: Orienting an audience to an economic issue
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop the opening of a response that orients the audience to an economic issue using relevant economic concepts and terms.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot orient their audience to the issue will produce explanations that assume shared context and vocabulary, making their work inaccessible and communicatively ineffective. The orientation is also the point at which economic vocabulary is established — failures here cascade into imprecise use throughout the explanation.
criteria: Writes an opening that names the economic issue and its relevance to the audience
Uses at least two economic or business terms accurately in the opening

width.minimum: Write an opening paragraph that names the issue, identifies the audience, and uses at least two economic terms accurately.
width.typical: Develop a response opening that orients the audience (peers or community members) to the economic issue — introducing the issue, explaining its relevance, and using economic and business concepts and terms such as market, income, business, goods and services, costs and benefits accurately and purposefully.
wider: Adapt the same economic issue explanation for two different audiences — for example, a Year 7 peer and an adult community member — comparing how vocabulary, detail level and framing shift
Evaluate a sample economic explanation for audience orientation: does it establish the issue clearly? Does the vocabulary suit the audience? What would improve it?
Develop an orientation for an economic issue affecting a specific community (e.g. a First Nations regional community) where the audience is community members rather than students

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding for how to open an economic explanation: name the issue, state why it matters, define any specialist terms the audience may not know, then proceed to the argument. Model this structure before students apply it independently.

nodes.label: Explaining with data and appropriate formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain ideas and decisions with details and examples, using data and information presented in appropriate formats — visual displays, tables, graphs, budget and savings plans.
criteria: Explains an idea or decision using at least one piece of referenced data or information
Presents data or information in a format appropriate to the explanation and audience
Uses economic and business terms (market, income, goods and services, costs and benefits) accurately throughout

width.minimum: Explain one idea or decision using at least one piece of data or information from a source, presented in an appropriate format (table, graph, or visual display).
width.typical: Explain ideas and decisions with details and examples, using data and information presented in appropriate formats — visual displays, tables, graphs, budget and savings plans, research findings in graphic organisers or summaries; select the format that best supports the explanation for the intended audience.
wider: Produce an explanation that integrates multiple data formats — for example, a written explanation supported by a graph and a budget plan — and evaluate which format added most value
Develop an explanation in a multi-modal format (e.g. a short presentation or infographic) that combines written explanation with data visualisation, targeting a specific audience

Create an explanation of an economic issue facing a First Nations community that draws on community-sourced data or reports, presenting the data in a format that respects and centres community context

modes.reason: Students need practice with multiple formats before they can select the most appropriate one for a given audience and explanation type. Provide structured opportunities to use each format type — table, graph, budget, visual display — and have students reflect on which worked best for their explanation.

descriptors.title: Markets and price signals
descriptors.description: how markets influence decisions about the allocation of resources to the production of goods and services, and the effect of prices on these decisions
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand why opportunity cost exists as decisions are made to allocate limited resources to meet unlimited needs and wants (AC9HE7K01). They understand the reasons businesses exist and how different types of businesses provide goods and services (AC9HE7K02).

nodes.label: Market participants and interactions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main participants in a market system (household, business, finance and government sectors) and describe how their interactions enable the market to function.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding who participates and how interactions work, students cannot meaningfully interpret what prices signal or how resource allocation decisions are made — both subsequent nodes depend on this foundation.
criteria: Identifies at least three of the four market sectors by name and describes a role each plays
Describes at least one interaction between sectors using appropriate economic terms (e.g. labour, income, goods, services)

width.minimum: Identify two or more sectors involved in the Australian market system and describe one interaction between them (e.g. households supply labour to businesses in exchange for income).
width.typical: Explain how the interactions of all four sectors — household, business, finance and government — enable the market to operate, including exchange of goods, services, labour and money flows.
wider: Map circular flow of income model showing all four sector interactions, including injections (government spending, investment, exports) and leakages (taxation, saving, imports)
Compare how market participation differs across different types of economies (e.g. mixed economy in Australia versus more command-oriented or subsistence contexts)
Investigate how digital platforms have created new forms of market participation, such as peer-to-peer transactions that blur the household/business sector boundary

modes.reason: Students often conflate the sectors or treat the government as external to the market rather than as an active participant. Explicitly mapping each sector's role and the flows between them builds the mental model needed for price signal reasoning.

nodes.label: The three allocation questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the interaction between buyers and sellers determines answers to 'What to produce?', 'How to produce?' and 'For whom to produce?'
nodes.hinge_reason: The three allocation questions are the conceptual frame for the descriptor's endpoint. If students cannot connect buyer-seller interactions to these questions, they cannot meaningfully explain resource allocation — the final node cannot be reached.
criteria: Names all three fundamental allocation questions and explains what each asks
Provides a specific example of how buyer-seller interaction answers at least two of the three allocation questions

width.minimum: Explain one of the three allocation questions (what, how, or for whom) using a specific example of buyer-seller interaction in a familiar market.
width.typical: Explain how buyer-seller interactions in markets provide answers to all three fundamental allocation questions, using concrete examples for each (e.g. rising demand for electric vehicles signals 'what' to produce; automation decisions address 'how'; income levels shape 'for whom').
wider: Investigate how market failures (e.g. negative externalities, public goods) mean markets sometimes give incomplete or distorted answers to the allocation questions, and how government intervention attempts to correct this
Compare how a command economy answers the three allocation questions centrally versus how a market economy decentralises those decisions to buyers and sellers
Explore how First Nations Australian community economies may answer allocation questions through non-market mechanisms such as reciprocity, kinship obligations and communal decision-making

modes.reason: The three questions are often reduced to slogans rather than applied analytically. Structured examples — 'When X happens in the market, what allocation question does that answer and why?' — build the analytical link needed.

Using multiple real-world market contexts (petrol, housing, food delivery) prevents students from treating the three questions as abstract; each context illuminates a different facet of how markets allocate.

nodes.label: Factors that influence price
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain multiple factors that influence how a price is set, using a concrete product or service example.
criteria: Names at least two distinct factors that influence the price of a specific product
Explains how a change in one of those factors would affect the price, using economic reasoning

width.minimum: Identify at least two factors that influence the price of one product or service and explain how each factor affects the price (e.g. petrol: supply availability and consumer demand).
width.typical: Discuss multiple factors that influence price-setting across different product contexts, including supply availability, consumer demand, production costs, and competition. Explain how these factors interact rather than operate in isolation.
wider: Investigate how global commodity prices (e.g. iron ore, wheat) influence domestic Australian prices and what factors drive price volatility on global markets
Examine how monopoly or oligopoly market structures allow businesses to set prices differently from competitive markets, and the consumer implications
Research how government intervention (excise taxes, subsidies, price controls) deliberately distorts prices away from where market forces would otherwise set them, and why

modes.reason: Students benefit from accumulating several concrete product-price examples before the integration node. Each example should add a different dominant factor (demand-driven, cost-driven, competition-driven) to build range.

nodes.label: Price as resource allocation signal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how price changes signal to consumers and businesses, and how those signals redirect resources toward or away from the production of specific goods and services.
criteria: Identifies a price change and explains the direction of the signal it sends to producers or consumers
Explains how a resource (labour, materials, capital) is redirected as a result of that price signal

width.minimum: Explain one example of how a rise or fall in price acts as a signal that causes consumers or businesses to change their behaviour, resulting in resources being redirected.
width.typical: Explain how price signals interact: when the price of a good or service rises, producers have incentive to redirect resources to produce more of it; when price falls, resources shift away. Use at least two examples showing both consumer and producer responses.
wider: Investigate how price signals in labour markets (wages) redirect human resources between industries over time — e.g. declining manufacturing wages versus rising technology sector wages in Australia
Analyse a real case study of rapid price change (e.g. mask prices during COVID-19, used car prices post-pandemic) to trace how resources were allocated in response to the price signal
Examine the concept of price elasticity: how the strength of the resource-allocation response to a price signal varies depending on how essential the good is and how many substitutes exist

modes.reason: Price-as-signal is an abstract mechanism. Multiple vivid real-world examples — including ones students have encountered (fuel, food, housing) — are needed to make the mechanism concrete before it can be applied at integration.

nodes.label: Markets, prices and resource allocation — integrated
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how markets influence decisions about the allocation of resources to the production of goods and services, connecting participant interactions, the three allocation questions, price factors, and price signals into a coherent account.
criteria: Explains how a market scenario connects participant interaction, pricing factors, and resource allocation decisions
Uses at least three economics terms accurately in an extended explanation of how markets influence resource allocation

width.minimum: Explain how a change in market conditions (e.g. a rise in consumer demand for a product) flows through the market system — affecting price, sending signals to producers, and ultimately redirecting resources. Use appropriate economic terms throughout.
width.typical: Explain how markets allocate resources through the price mechanism, drawing on all four building blocks: who participates and how, the three allocation questions, what drives prices, and how price signals direct resource flows. Apply to at least one extended example.
wider: Compare how the market allocates resources in a sector experiencing rapid technological change (e.g. energy, transport) versus a more stable sector, examining how the price signals differ in strength and speed

Investigate a case where market price signals have led to outcomes that are efficient for producers and consumers but problematic for society (e.g. environmental costs not captured in price), and explain why the market allocation is incomplete
Evaluate how First Nations Australian businesses use market signals alongside non-market values (Country stewardship, community benefit) when making production and resource allocation decisions

modes.reason: The four building blocks from earlier nodes must be connected into a single coherent explanation. Students should demonstrate they can trace a cause from market conditions through to resource allocation, not treat each concept as a separate item.

descriptors.title: Business adaptation
descriptors.description: different ways that businesses adapt to opportunities in the market and respond to the changing nature of work
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the reasons businesses exist and how different types of businesses provide goods and services (AC9HE7K02). They understand entrepreneur characteristics and how these influence business success (AC9HE7K03). They understand how markets allocate resources through price signals (AC9HE8K01).

nodes.label: Identifying market opportunities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how businesses identify needs, niches and gaps in established markets and how these guide the development of new products or services.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how businesses identify opportunities is the foundation for explaining both technology-driven adaptation and workforce change — students who cannot explain this link will treat later nodes as disconnected examples rather than a coherent picture of business adaptation.
criteria: Identifies a market need, niche or gap that a real business responded to
Explains how identifying that opportunity influenced what the business decided to produce or offer

width.minimum: Identify one example of a business that identified a gap or niche in the market and explain how that opportunity guided what it produced or offered.
width.typical: Explain how businesses systematically identify needs, niches and gaps in established markets, and how this analysis shapes the development of specific goods or services. Use two or more examples drawn from different market sectors (e.g. electric vehicles, solar energy, health tech).
wider: Investigate how market research methods (surveys, data analytics, focus groups) help businesses identify opportunities before a product or service exists

Examine how disruptive innovations create entirely new market categories rather than filling existing gaps — e.g. how streaming services did not just fill a gap in DVD rental but eliminated the category
Research how social enterprises and not-for-profit businesses identify opportunities that traditional profit-seeking businesses overlook, particularly in underserved communities

modes.reason: Students need a range of concrete business examples — across industries and scales — to see that opportunity identification is a generalised business behaviour, not a quirk of specific companies. Build the repertoire before asking for analysis.

nodes.label: Technology-driven business adaptation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how businesses use technologies to streamline operations or gain efficiencies, using specific examples such as ride share, food delivery and online retail.
criteria: Names a specific technology a business adopted and describes the efficiency or market opportunity it created
Explains the connection between the technology adoption and the business's ability to serve customers or compete in the market

width.minimum: Describe how one business has used a specific technology to streamline its operations or improve efficiency, naming the technology and the efficiency gained.
width.typical: Explain how businesses across different sectors use technologies to streamline or gain efficiencies in existing business models, including platform-based models (ride share, food delivery apps) and online retail. Discuss both the business benefit and the market opportunity created.
wider: Investigate how automation and artificial intelligence are being adopted by Australian businesses (e.g. retail checkout, logistics, accounting) and the efficiency gains and workforce implications
Examine how data analytics and algorithmic tools allow businesses to personalise offerings at scale — e.g. streaming recommendations, targeted advertising, dynamic pricing

Compare how a traditional business model in one sector (e.g. taxi industry, physical retail) was disrupted by a technology-enabled competitor, analysing what the incumbent was slow to adapt to and why

modes.reason: Students often confine technology adaptation to the most prominent examples (Uber, Amazon). Wider sector examples reveal that technology-driven efficiency is a cross-industry pattern, not a Silicon Valley phenomenon.

nodes.label: Changing nature of work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain current and historical influences on how people work, including technological change, globalisation, communication changes and workforce casualisation.
criteria: Names at least two distinct influences on the changing nature of work
Explains, using a specific example, how one of these influences has changed the way a type of work is performed or organised in Australia

width.minimum: Identify and explain two influences on the changing nature of work in Australia (e.g. technological change and casualisation), giving at least one concrete example for each.
width.typical: Explain multiple influences on the ways people work including: technological change, outsourced labour in the global economy, rapid communication changes, and casualisation of the workforce. Use specific Australian examples and explain how each influence changes employment arrangements or job types.
wider: Investigate changes to the Australian workforce over time using data: jobs growth and decline across industries, changing career length patterns, and shifting demographic composition of the workforce

Examine the gig economy in Australia — the rights and responsibilities of workers in platform-mediated casual work (ride share, food delivery, freelance platforms) and the policy debates around classification as employees vs. contractors
Research how corporate social responsibility, sustainability practices and changing consumer values are influencing what kinds of work businesses create and how they manage human resources

modes.reason: The descriptor lists four distinct influences. Students need grounded examples of each before they can discuss the descriptor's full scope. Build the repertoire of influence-type → example pairs before synthesis.

nodes.label: Business adaptation — integrated
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss how businesses adapt to market opportunities and the changing nature of work, connecting opportunity identification, technology use, and workforce change into a coherent account of business adaptation.
criteria: Discusses at least two ways a business adapts to opportunities or changing work conditions
Connects the business's adaptation choices to a specific market opportunity or work-related change, using appropriate terminology

width.minimum: Discuss how one business has responded to both a market opportunity and the changing nature of work, explaining how these two dimensions of adaptation are connected.
width.typical: Discuss how businesses adapt to market opportunities and respond to changes in the nature of work, drawing on the full range of adaptation types: identifying gaps, deploying technology, and restructuring how work is organised. Use at least two detailed examples.
wider: Evaluate how a business's adaptation strategy has created benefits for some stakeholders (shareholders, consumers) while creating costs or disruptions for others (workers displaced by automation, local suppliers replaced by global outsourcing)
Investigate how a First Nations Australian business has adapted to market opportunities in ways that integrate cultural values and responsibilities to Country alongside commercial goals
Research a business that failed to adapt — analyse what opportunities or changes it missed and what the consequences were for the business, its workers, and its market

modes.reason: Students should demonstrate that market opportunity identification, technology adoption, and workforce change are not three separate topics but interconnected dimensions of how businesses respond to their environment. The integration task should require connecting at least two of these.

descriptors.title: First Nations enterprise
descriptors.description: how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs develop opportunities in the market
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the reasons businesses exist and characteristics of entrepreneurs (AC9HE7K02, AC9HE7K03). They have context from AC9HE8K02 on how businesses identify market opportunities and adapt.

nodes.label: First Nations business structures and partnerships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs establish partnerships or cooperatives to provide goods and services, including in sectors such as farming, fashion, design or tourism.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that First Nations businesses operate through distinct structural models (cooperatives, community enterprises, partnerships grounded in communal obligation) will misread the next node — treating participation in contemporary markets as identical to mainstream business participation rather than understanding the additional barriers and distinctive strategies involved.
criteria: Identifies a specific First Nations Australian business or cooperative and describes its structure
Explains how the partnership or cooperative arrangement supports the provision of goods or services in that business

width.minimum: Investigate one First Nations Australian business or cooperative and explain how it is structured, what goods or services it provides, and how partnerships or collective arrangements support it.
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australian businesses establish partnerships or cooperatives to provide goods and services across different sectors (farming, fashion, design, cultural tourism). Explain how collective and partnership models reflect community values alongside commercial operation.
wider: Compare the cooperative business model used by some First Nations communities with mainstream investor-owned business structures, examining what each optimises for (profit, community benefit, cultural maintenance)

Investigate how Indigenous Land Use Agreements (ILUAs) and native title mechanisms have enabled First Nations businesses to enter markets in land management, environmental services and resource sectors
Research a First Nations fashion or design business and investigate how intellectual property and cultural ownership questions intersect with commercial activity

modes.reason: Students may default to evaluating First Nations businesses against mainstream profit-maximising norms. Structured reasoning about different business purposes — community benefit, cultural maintenance, economic participation — establishes the frame needed before market participation is examined.

nodes.label: Participation in contemporary markets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian communities participate in contemporary markets, including how they produce, buy and sell goods and services and the strategies they use to overcome difficulties in accessing markets.
criteria: Describes at least one way a First Nations community or business participates in a contemporary market
Identifies at least one barrier to market access and explains a strategy used to address it

width.minimum: Explain one way that a First Nations Australian community or business participates in a contemporary market, and identify at least one difficulty they face in accessing that market.
width.typical: Explain how First Nations Australian communities participate in contemporary markets: producing, buying and selling goods and services; approaches to marketing, employment and social contribution; and strategies used to overcome difficulties in accessing markets (e.g. remoteness, capital access, cultural protocols in business contexts).
wider: Investigate how digital platforms and e-commerce have opened new market access pathways for First Nations businesses in remote and regional areas that face geographic barriers to mainstream markets
