Research the role of organisations such as Supply Nation in supporting First Nations businesses to access government and corporate procurement markets
Examine how tourism provides economic participation opportunities for First Nations communities and the tensions between commercial tourism and cultural and environmental custodianship

modes.reason: First Nations market participation spans urban businesses, remote community enterprises, cultural tourism, and digital trade. Multiple contexts prevent students from treating one case study as representative of a diverse and geographically varied economic reality.

nodes.label: Connection to Country as economic innovation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs use connection to, and responsibility for, Country/Place to make innovations in the production and distribution of goods and services.
criteria: Identifies a specific First Nations business innovation that draws on Country/Place knowledge or connection
Explains how the innovation creates market value while reflecting responsibilities to Country/Place

width.minimum: Describe one example of a First Nations business innovation that draws on knowledge of, or responsibility for, Country/Place — such as medicines, food products, environmental services or cultural tourism — and explain how Country/Place connection is central to the innovation.
width.typical: Explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs use connection to Country/Place as the basis for innovation in production and distribution, including examples such as bush food and medicine products, cultural tourism, environmental monitoring, and design. Explain how this knowledge creates market value while maintaining cultural obligations.
wider: Investigate the bush food and native ingredient industry in Australia — how First Nations knowledge of plants and their uses is being commercialised, and what intellectual property, benefit-sharing and cultural authority questions this raises

Research how First Nations-led environmental and conservation enterprises (e.g. carbon farming, ranger programs, fire management) generate income from Country/Place knowledge in ways that integrate economic and custodial responsibilities

Compare how connection to Country as an economic asset is legally recognised and protected (e.g. through native title, geographic indications, cultural heritage law) versus how it remains vulnerable to appropriation without adequate protection

modes.reason: Country/Place connection as economic innovation is genuinely diverse — food, medicine, tourism, environmental services, design. Multiple contexts prevent reduction to a single example and reveal the breadth of economic activity grounded in this relationship.

descriptors.title: Taxation and decision-making
descriptors.description: the importance of Australia's system of taxation and how this system affects decision-making by individuals and businesses
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand why individuals work and how income is derived (AC9HE7K04). They understand consumer rights and financial responsibilities (AC9HE7K05). They have foundational knowledge of how market prices affect decision-making (AC9HE8K01).

nodes.label: Why taxation exists
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why the Australian government collects taxation revenue and the types of services this revenue funds for individuals and communities.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not understand the purpose and scope of taxation revenue, they cannot meaningfully reason about how the taxation system affects decision-making — subsequent nodes on rights/obligations and tax's effect on prices rest on this foundation.
criteria: Explains at least one reason why the Australian government collects taxation revenue
Names at least three government services funded by taxation and identifies who benefits from each

width.minimum: Explain why the government collects taxation revenue and name at least three types of government services funded by taxation (e.g. health, education, infrastructure).
width.typical: Discuss why the government collects taxation revenue and explain how it funds services for individuals and communities including health, education, paid parental leave, childcare, aged care and infrastructure. Explain how taxation redistributes resources across the population.
wider: Investigate the relative size of different categories of Australian government spending (health, education, social security, defence) and compare the proportion funded by taxation versus other government revenue
Examine the concept of progressive taxation and why Australia uses it — the argument that those with higher capacity to pay should contribute proportionally more to public services

Research how public goods and services that are non-excludable and non-rival (e.g. national defence, public parks) cannot be efficiently provided by markets alone, making taxation-funded provision necessary

modes.reason: Students often arrive with normative views on taxation (it's unfair, it's necessary) without understanding the structural reasoning. Establishing the public goods and redistribution rationale before examining mechanics prevents the later nodes being reduced to opinion.

nodes.label: How and when individuals pay tax
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain when and how young Australians pay tax, including income tax calculation, tax file numbers, employer deductions and lodging a tax return.
criteria: Explains what a tax file number is and identifies when a young Australian should apply for one
Describes the process by which income tax is deducted from wages, including the employer's role

width.minimum: Explain what a tax file number is, when a young Australian needs to apply for one, and how income tax is deducted from wages by an employer.
width.typical: Explain when and why young Australians pay tax: applying for a tax file number, how income tax is calculated from income brackets, how employers deduct and remit tax, and how to lodge a tax return including what happens when too much or too little tax has been deducted.
wider: Investigate the Australian income tax bracket system and calculate income tax for different income levels, exploring why the effective tax rate (total tax as a percentage of income) increases with income
Examine the role of the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and myGov in administering income tax — including what data the ATO automatically receives and the process for pre-filling tax returns

Research the rights and obligations in the tax system: what taxpayers are entitled to (e.g. deductions for work-related expenses) and what they are obligated to do (accurate reporting, timely lodgement)

modes.reason: This node has procedural elements (TFN application, PAYG deductions, tax return lodgement) where students benefit from practising the steps and the vocabulary accurately. Errors here (e.g. confusing gross income, taxable income and net income) propagate into the decision-making analysis nodes.

nodes.label: Types of tax and their effect on prices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify examples of taxes paid by individuals and businesses and explain how they may influence spending and pricing decisions.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of taxes and who pays each
Explains, with a specific example, how one tax type influences a decision made by an individual or business

width.minimum: Identify two different types of taxes (e.g. income tax, GST, excise duty) and explain how one of them influences a spending or pricing decision.
width.typical: Identify examples of taxes paid by individuals and businesses — including income tax, GST, import duties and excise duties — and explain how each may influence decision-making about spending and pricing. Use specific product examples (e.g. how excise on alcohol or petrol affects consumer purchasing).
wider: Investigate how the GST (Goods and Services Tax) operates as a value-added consumption tax, including which goods and services are exempt and why (fresh food, health, education) and the distributional consequences of a flat consumption tax

Research how tariffs and import duties are used as both revenue-raising measures and policy instruments to protect domestic industries, and how these affect consumer prices and business sourcing decisions

Examine how businesses factor taxation (company tax, payroll tax, GST obligations) into pricing decisions, and why the incidence of a tax (who ultimately bears the cost) may differ from who formally pays it

modes.reason: Different tax types have qualitatively different effects on decisions — income tax affects labour supply decisions, excise affects consumption of specific goods, import duties affect sourcing decisions. Each context type needs representation to reach the descriptor's full scope.

nodes.label: Taxation, wellbeing and decision-making — integrated
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the importance of Australia's taxation system — connecting revenue purpose, individual obligations, tax types and their effects on decisions — and explain how the system supports individual and community wellbeing.
criteria: Explains why Australia's taxation system is important, referencing both revenue purposes and the services it funds
Explains how at least one feature of the taxation system affects decision-making by an individual or a business

width.minimum: Explain how Australia's taxation system affects a decision made by a young person (e.g. whether and how much to work, what to spend money on) and connect this to how the system funds services that support wellbeing.
width.typical: Explain the importance of the Australian taxation system by connecting: why taxation exists and what it funds; how individuals meet their tax obligations; how different types of taxes affect spending and pricing decisions; and how the system collectively supports individual human and financial wellbeing, communities and Australian society.
wider: Evaluate whether the current Australian tax mix is well-designed to achieve its goals — examining arguments for and against changes (e.g. raising or lowering income tax, extending or narrowing the GST base, introducing new taxes on wealth or carbon)
Research how Australia's taxation revenue as a proportion of GDP compares with comparable countries (OECD nations) and what this implies about the scope of government services each provides

Investigate a case where a tax has been deliberately used to change behaviour (e.g. carbon pricing, tobacco excise, sugar tax proposals) and evaluate evidence on whether it achieved its intended effect

modes.reason: The integration task should require students to connect taxation's purpose (funding services) with its mechanics (how it is collected) and its effects (how it shapes decisions) — not treat these as separate items. A real scenario (a young person starting work, a business setting a price) is a useful integration frame.

descriptors.title: Planning and budgeting
descriptors.description: processes that individuals and/or businesses use to plan and budget to achieve short-term and long-term financial objectives
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand consumer rights and financial responsibilities (AC9HE7K05). They understand income sources and the reasons individuals work (AC9HE7K04). They have context from AC9HE8K04 on how the taxation system affects individual financial decisions.

nodes.label: Personal financial objectives and planning tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ways that short-term and long-term personal financial objectives can be achieved, including through developing a budget and savings plan.
nodes.hinge_reason: The personal financial planning node establishes the conceptual frame (short-term vs long-term objectives; planning as a process not a one-off decision) that the business financial planning node builds on. Students who have only encountered budgeting as a static document rather than a dynamic planning process will not connect it to the business tools in the next node.
criteria: Distinguishes between a short-term and long-term personal financial objective
Explains how a budget or savings plan can be used to work toward a specific financial objective

width.minimum: Identify one short-term and one long-term personal financial objective and explain one process (e.g. a budget or savings plan) that could help achieve each.
width.typical: Identify ways that short-term and long-term personal financial objectives can be achieved, explaining how tools such as a personal budget and savings plan work, and how they can be adapted to different income and expenditure situations.
wider: Investigate how interest rates affect personal saving and borrowing decisions — calculating the effect of compound interest on a savings target over different timeframes
Examine how life stage affects financial planning priorities: comparing the financial objectives and planning tools relevant to a young person starting work versus someone approaching retirement
Research how financial literacy interventions in schools affect long-term financial wellbeing outcomes, and evaluate what financial skills are most important to develop early

modes.reason: Budget construction is a procedural skill with common errors (confusing income and expenditure categories, conflating savings with surplus). Students benefit from practising with real-number scenarios before the concept is extended to business contexts.

nodes.label: Business financial records and decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how financial records — including income statements, balance sheets, budgets and cash flow statements — inform business decision-making.
criteria: Names at least two types of business financial records and describes the different information each provides
Explains how one type of financial record informs a specific business decision

width.minimum: Explain what one type of business financial record (e.g. an income statement or cash flow statement) shows, and describe one decision a business might make based on that information.
width.typical: Explain how financial records — income statements, balance sheets, budgets and cash flow statements — each provide different information that informs different types of business decision-making (profitability, solvency, planning, liquidity). Explain how reading these records together gives a more complete picture of financial health.
wider: Investigate how investors and lenders use business financial statements to assess risk before providing capital — examining what each record signals about a business's financial position

Examine a real Australian publicly listed company's annual report, identifying what the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement reveal and any financial risks or opportunities they suggest
Research how accounting standards and audit requirements create trust in financial records — and what happens when financial records are manipulated (e.g. corporate accounting scandals)

modes.reason: Students often confuse the four record types (particularly income statement vs balance sheet vs cash flow). Explicit structural comparison — what question does each document answer? what time period does it cover? — prevents conflation and builds transferable financial literacy.

nodes.label: Business planning processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain business processes used to manage finances and plan in the short and long term, including business plans, borrowing from financial institutions and building savings through interest.
criteria: Identifies at least two business processes used for financial planning or management
Explains how one of these processes helps a business work toward a short-term or long-term financial objective

width.minimum: Identify one short-term and one long-term business financial planning process and explain how each helps a business manage its finances toward an objective.
width.typical: Identify and explain business processes used for short-term and long-term financial planning: devising a business plan, borrowing from financial institutions to fund growth or operations, and building savings through earned interest. Explain how each process serves a different planning horizon or financial need.
wider: Investigate the components of a business plan and why banks and investors require them before providing finance — examining what a business plan signals about financial preparedness and risk
Research how small businesses in Australia access finance through different channels (bank loans, microfinance, crowdfunding, government grants) and the advantages and constraints of each

Examine how a business uses break-even analysis as a planning tool — calculating the volume of sales needed to cover costs and what this means for short-term survival and long-term investment decisions

modes.reason: Business planning processes are easiest to understand through concrete cases — a start-up seeking a bank loan, an established business building a reserve fund, a growing business with a multi-year investment plan. Different scenarios illustrate different planning horizons.

nodes.label: Planning and budgeting — integrated
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how individuals and businesses use planning and budgeting processes to achieve short-term and long-term financial objectives, drawing on appropriate financial records and planning tools.
criteria: Explains the difference between a short-term and long-term financial objective in a realistic scenario
Identifies and explains at least two planning or budgeting processes an individual or business could use to achieve those objectives

width.minimum: Explain how either an individual or a business would use at least two planning or budgeting processes together to work toward a stated financial objective.
width.typical: Explain how individuals and businesses use a connected set of planning and budgeting processes — combining personal budgets, savings plans, business financial records and business planning tools — to achieve both short-term and long-term financial objectives. Apply to a scenario involving real financial decisions.
wider: Analyse a scenario where short-term and long-term objectives are in tension (e.g. spending now to grow a business versus building financial resilience) and evaluate how planning tools help manage that trade-off

Investigate how financial planning processes differ for a First Nations community-owned enterprise, where objectives include community wellbeing and cultural maintenance alongside financial sustainability
Research financial planning challenges faced by young Australians entering the workforce today (housing affordability, superannuation, study debt) and evaluate which planning tools are most relevant

modes.reason: The integration task should require connecting personal financial planning (budget, savings plan) with business financial planning (records, business plan) around a concrete scenario, making explicit that both use similar principles at different scales.

descriptors.title: Develop inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue (AC9HE7S01). At Year 8, the expectation shifts toward questions that are more precisely targeted using economics and business concepts and terms, and toward a wider range of issue types.

nodes.label: Broad and targeted question types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between broad inquiry questions and targeted questions that use economics and business concepts and terms, and explain why targeted questions produce more useful investigations.
nodes.hinge_reason: The distinction between broad and targeted questions determines the quality of all subsequent inquiry work — students who cannot frame targeted questions will produce unfocused investigations and struggle to locate relevant evidence in subsequent skill nodes.
criteria: Develops at least one question using an economics or business concept or term accurately
Explains why a targeted concept-driven question is more useful for investigation than a broad question about the same issue

width.minimum: Identify one example of a broad question and one targeted question about the same economic or business issue; explain what makes the targeted question more useful for investigation.
width.typical: Develop a range of questions for an investigation — including broad framing questions and targeted questions using economics and business concepts and terms (e.g. 'How is the price of goods and services determined?' and 'Why do changes in market price act as a signal about how scarce resources should be allocated?'). Explain what each type of question contributes to the investigation.
wider: Compare the same economic issue investigated using only broad questions versus targeted concept-driven questions, and evaluate the difference in the depth and usefulness of evidence gathered

Practise converting everyday observations ('things are getting more expensive') into precise economic questions using specific concepts ('How does the relationship between supply and demand explain recent changes in housing rental prices in Australia?')
Investigate how professional economists and journalists frame questions differently about the same issue, and analyse what the different framings reveal about their purposes

modes.reason: The shift from 'why does X happen?' to a concept-anchored question requires understanding what economic concepts are available and what question type produces useful evidence. Explicit scaffolding — listing relevant concepts, then asking 'which concept does this issue involve?' — develops the targeting habit.

nodes.label: Developing a question set for investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a range of questions — forming the basis of an investigation — that together enable systematic inquiry into a contemporary economic and business issue.
criteria: Develops a set of at least two questions that together address different dimensions of a contemporary economic or business issue
At least one question accurately uses an economics or business concept or term as the basis for inquiry

width.minimum: Develop at least two questions that together form the basis of an investigation into one contemporary economic or business issue — including at least one targeted concept-driven question.
width.typical: Develop a set of questions that form the basis of an investigation into a contemporary economic and business issue. The set should include framing questions (e.g. 'Why does X happen?'), targeted questions using economics and business concepts and terms, and questions about the issue's effects on different stakeholders.
wider: Develop question sets for two different types of economic issues (a market pricing issue and a business adaptation issue) and compare how the required question types differ
Evaluate a peer's question set against criteria: Are the questions investigable? Do they use concepts accurately? Do they lead to different types of evidence? Revise based on the evaluation
Investigate a real economic report or parliamentary inquiry submission and reverse-engineer the question set that appears to have driven the investigation

modes.reason: Question development improves through repeated practice across different issue types. Students benefit from developing question sets for multiple issues before the skill is assessed — each iteration adds to their repertoire of question patterns.

descriptors.title: Locate and organise information
descriptors.description: locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources (AC9HE7S02). At Year 8, the expectation shifts toward more advanced search strategies, explicit source evaluation, and using specialised digital tools to organise data.

nodes.label: Locating and evaluating sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate information from a range of sources using advanced search strategies and evaluate the relevance of sources by asking whether the data or information helps answer the inquiry question.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot locate credible and relevant sources, they cannot produce evidence-based analysis in subsequent nodes. Poor source selection undermines every downstream skill — interpretation, response development and communication all depend on the quality of what has been found.
criteria: Uses at least one search strategy beyond a basic keyword search to locate relevant information
Identifies whether a source is relevant to the inquiry question and explains the reason

width.minimum: Use at least one advanced search strategy (e.g. specifying site type or search terms in quotation marks) to locate information on an economic or business issue, and explain why the source found is or is not relevant to the inquiry question.
width.typical: Locate information and data from a range of source types (government departments, non-government organisations, news media, statistics agencies) using advanced search functions. Evaluate sources by asking 'How will this data or information help answer the question?' and filter out sources that do not contribute to the investigation.
wider: Compare the same economic issue as reported by different source types (e.g. ABS data, a business news article, an NGO report) and evaluate what each source type can and cannot reliably tell you
Investigate how to assess source credibility for economic and business data — examining indicators of authority, currency, methodology and potential bias
Research how economists and researchers use primary data sources (ABS, RBA, ASIC) versus secondary commentary, and practise tracing a claim in a secondary source back to its primary data

modes.reason: Search strategies are procedural and benefit from repeated practice with explicit feedback. Students often over-rely on first-result web searches and need to practise the habit of source type targeting (government statistics, NGO reports, industry data) before it becomes automatic.

nodes.label: Selecting and organising data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select relevant information and data from located sources and organise it into appropriate formats — including diagrams or tables — using specialised digital tools.
criteria: Selects information from at least two sources and explains why each was selected as relevant
Organises the selected data in a format (table, diagram, or other) that makes relationships or comparisons visible

width.minimum: Select relevant information from at least two sources and organise it into one format (e.g. a table or diagram) that makes the relationship between the data clear.
width.typical: Select relevant information and data from multiple sources and organise it using appropriate formats — including diagrams modelling economic relationships (e.g. market interactions) and tables comparing features of different business types or strategies. Use specialised digital tools (e.g. spreadsheet, diagram tool) where appropriate.
wider: Construct a relational diagram (e.g. circular flow model, supply and demand diagram, market ecosystem map) that accurately represents the economic or business relationships in the data found

Organise data from multiple sources into a comparative table that enables direct comparison of features across multiple cases (e.g. features of different business models, tax rates across countries, wage trends by industry)
Evaluate two different organisational formats for the same data set (e.g. table vs diagram) and justify which is more useful for the investigation's inquiry question

modes.reason: Different economic inquiry questions require different organisational formats. Students benefit from practising multiple formats — comparison tables, flow diagrams, data summaries — to build a repertoire they can select from based on what the investigation requires.

descriptors.title: Interpret economic data
descriptors.description: interpret information and data to identify economic and business issues, trends and economic cause-and-effect relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret information and data to identify economic and business issues, trends and cause-and-effect relationships (AC9HE7S03). At Year 8, the expectation develops toward interpreting multi-variable data and identifying cause-and-effect relationships within economic and business issues.

nodes.label: Interpreting to identify issues and signals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret information to identify economic and business issues, including inferring what a change in price or expenditure signals about an underlying economic condition.
nodes.hinge_reason: The move from 'what does this show?' to 'what does this signal about an underlying condition?' is the interpretive step that distinguishes economic analysis from description. Students who cannot make this move will not be able to identify cause-and-effect relationships in the subsequent node.
criteria: Identifies an economic or business issue from a data source, going beyond surface-level description
Infers what an observed change (in price, expenditure or other indicator) signals about an underlying economic condition

width.minimum: Interpret one piece of economic or business information (e.g. a news report, a data excerpt) and identify the economic or business issue it signals, using inference rather than just restating the surface content.
width.typical: Interpret information to identify economic and business issues, including inferring from indirect signals — e.g. a change in the price of a key commodity as a signal about resource scarcity, or increasing consumer expenditure as a signal about economic conditions. Distinguish between what the data shows directly and what it implies about underlying conditions.
wider: Practise interpreting economic signals that are counterintuitive — e.g. why rising unemployment sometimes follows interest rate cuts, or why a falling exchange rate can simultaneously help exporters and hurt importers
Investigate how economic indicators (e.g. CPI, unemployment rate, GDP growth) are used as signals about the state of the economy and what policy responses they typically trigger
Compare how two different sources interpret the same economic data differently, and analyse what assumptions or perspectives drive the different interpretations

modes.reason: Signal-reading requires a two-step habit: (1) state what the data shows, then (2) ask 'what economic condition would produce this pattern?' Scaffolding this explicitly — with structured prompts rather than open-ended questions — builds the inference habit needed for multi-variable interpretation.

nodes.label: Reading trends from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret data displayed in tables and graphs to identify trends over time and use those trends to answer a specific inquiry question.
criteria: Identifies the trend in a provided data set and states the direction and approximate magnitude of change
Uses the trend to answer a specific inquiry question accurately

width.minimum: Read a graph or table showing economic data over time, identify the trend, and use that trend to answer one specific inquiry question.
width.typical: Interpret data displayed in tables and graphs to identify trends and answer targeted questions (e.g. 'For a 10-year period, what is the trend in the percentage of people over 60 paying income tax?'). Distinguish between short-term fluctuations and long-term trends, and explain what the trend suggests about the underlying economic or business condition.
wider: Practise reading trend data that reverses or contains anomalies (e.g. a trend that is interrupted by a recession or pandemic) and analyse what caused the deviation from trend
Investigate how to calculate percentage change and compound growth rate from trend data, and apply these to compare the rate of change across two different economic variables
Research how trend data from different sources (ABS, RBA, OECD) can give different pictures of the same phenomenon depending on the time period, unit of measurement or sample selected

modes.reason: Graph and table reading is procedural and error-prone (misreading axes, confusing levels with rates of change, ignoring units). Repeated practice with different data formats and explicit error-correction builds the precision needed before multi-variable interpretation.

nodes.label: Interpreting multi-variable cause-and-effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret multi-variable data to identify a cause-and-effect relationship within an economic or business issue.
criteria: Identifies a cause-and-effect relationship in a multi-variable data set
Explains the economic mechanism that connects the cause to the effect, not just noting that the variables move together

width.minimum: Interpret two related variables in a data set (e.g. income earned and taxation paid, supply increase and price adjustment) and identify the cause-and-effect relationship between them.
width.typical: Interpret multi-variable data to identify cause-and-effect relationships within an economic or business issue — including examples such as: the relationship between income and taxation paid, and how supply increase causes price adjustment. Explain the mechanism connecting the cause to the effect, not just noting the correlation.
wider: Distinguish between correlation and causation in economic data, examining cases where two variables move together but the causal link is indirect, delayed, or mediated by a third variable
Analyse a multi-variable economic data set (e.g. unemployment, inflation and interest rates together) and trace how changes in one variable create effects in others through economic mechanisms

Evaluate the limits of cause-and-effect interpretation in economics — examining why economic relationships are context-dependent and why the same cause can produce different effects in different conditions

modes.reason: Cause-and-effect identification in multi-variable data requires students to explain the mechanism, not just identify the pattern. Structured reasoning prompts — 'What is causing what? Through what process? Under what conditions?' — prevent students from asserting causation without mechanistic explanation.

descriptors.title: Develop responses to issues
descriptors.description: develop a response to an economic and business issue, identifying potential costs and benefits
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop a response to an economic and business issue identifying potential costs and benefits (AC9HE7S04). At Year 8, the expectation develops toward responses that combine known knowledge with new ideas and that require explicit identification and description of costs and benefits.

nodes.label: Identifying costs and benefits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the potential costs and benefits of a decision, including non-financial dimensions, and explain what is foregone when a choice is made.
nodes.hinge_reason: Costs and benefits identification is the analytical foundation of the response. Students who conflate financial and non-financial costs, or who omit opportunity cost, will produce incomplete responses that do not meet the descriptor's demand for explicit cost-benefit reasoning.
criteria: Identifies at least one cost and one benefit of a specific economic or business decision
Explains what is foregone (opportunity cost) when the decision is made

width.minimum: Identify at least one potential cost and one potential benefit of a specific economic or business decision, and explain what is foregone (opportunity cost) when that decision is made.
width.typical: Identify and describe the potential costs and benefits of an economic or business decision — including financial and non-financial dimensions. Explain that making a decision involves choice and foregoing an alternative want, using appropriate examples (e.g. doing casual work involves benefits such as money earned and costs such as less certainty about work hours).
wider: Practise identifying costs and benefits from the perspectives of multiple stakeholders affected by the same decision — distinguishing private costs/benefits (to the decision-maker) from social costs/benefits (to the broader community)

Investigate how businesses systematically conduct cost-benefit analysis before major decisions, including how they handle costs and benefits that are hard to quantify (e.g. environmental impact, reputational risk)
Research a government policy decision (e.g. a new tax, infrastructure investment) and evaluate the costs and benefits identified in the official policy rationale versus critiques of that analysis

modes.reason: Students often list benefits without matching them with genuine costs, or identify only financial dimensions. Structured cost-benefit scaffolds — requiring equal treatment of each side and explicit consideration of opportunity cost — build balanced analysis before it is applied in a full response.

nodes.label: Developing a reasoned response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a response to an economic and business issue that combines known knowledge with new ideas, identifies and describes reasons informing a recommendation, and addresses the potential costs and benefits.
criteria: Develops a response that includes a position or recommendation on an economic or business issue
Identifies and describes at least one reason supporting the response and at least one potential cost and benefit of the recommended course of action

width.minimum: Develop a response to one economic or business issue that includes: a stated position or recommendation, at least one reason supporting it, and acknowledgement of at least one cost and one benefit.
width.typical: Develop a response to an economic and business issue that combines known knowledge with new ideas, identifies and describes the reasons informing a recommendation (e.g. why the government collects taxation revenue and provides services), and identifies the potential costs and benefits of the recommended course of action.
wider: Develop a response that evaluates two or more alternative courses of action against the same set of cost-benefit criteria, and justifies a recommendation by comparing across the alternatives

Apply a personal budget and savings plan to an issue (e.g. whether to purchase a good or service) as the basis for a response — demonstrating that a response can be grounded in personal financial planning processes

Develop a response to an issue that explicitly acknowledges whose costs and benefits are included and whose may be underweighted or omitted, and reflects on what that means for the quality of the response

modes.reason: Response development improves with practice across different issue types. Students benefit from developing responses to market pricing issues, business strategy issues, and personal financial issues before the full inquiry sequence is assessed.

descriptors.title: Create economic explanations
descriptors.description: create descriptions and explanations, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create descriptions and explanations using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources (AC9HE7S05). At Year 8, the expectation develops toward explicit orientation of the audience to the issue and more deliberate use of data to support conclusions.

nodes.label: Orienting an audience to an issue
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a response that orients the audience to an economic or business issue using relevant concepts and terms, establishing what the issue is, why it matters, and to whom.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot orient an audience to an issue tend to jump directly into their own knowledge or data, producing explanations that assume context the reader does not have. This undermines the communicative function of the entire response.
criteria: Identifies the economic or business issue clearly in an opening that orients the audience
Names at least one relevant economics or business concept or term in the orientation

width.minimum: Write an opening for an explanation that orients the audience to one economic or business issue — identifying the issue, naming the relevant economic concept(s), and establishing why the audience should care.
width.typical: Develop a response that orients the audience (e.g. peers or community groups) to the issue using relevant economic and business concepts and terms such as 'markets', 'business', 'consumer and financial decision-making' and 'taxation'. Establish what the issue is, why it matters, and who is affected before moving to the explanation.
wider: Adapt the same explanation for two different audiences (e.g. peers vs parents vs community group) and analyse how the opening orientation needs to change to match audience knowledge, values and stakes
Practise issue orientation in different formats — a written paragraph, a spoken introduction, an infographic opening — and evaluate which elements are common to all formats and which vary
Research how economic journalists and public policy communicators orient audiences to complex issues (e.g. Reserve Bank explainers, ABS data stories) and identify the structural features they use

modes.reason: Audience orientation requires students to think about what the reader does not already know — a perspective-taking move that many Year 8 students have not yet internalised as a writing habit. Explicit scaffolding (write one sentence stating the issue; one sentence explaining why it matters; one sentence identifying who is affected) builds the habit before it is applied in a full piece.

nodes.label: Using data and sources to support explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a description or explanation that uses data or information from sources in appropriate formats to support decisions and conclusions about an economic or business issue.
criteria: Creates an explanation that uses at least one piece of data or information from a source
Explains the connection between the cited data or information and the conclusion it supports

width.minimum: Create an explanation of one economic or business issue that references at least one piece of data or information from a source, and explains how that data supports a conclusion.
width.typical: Create a description or explanation using data or information presented in appropriate formats to support decisions and conclusions about an economic and business issue. Reference sources accurately, explain the connection between the data and the conclusion, and use economic and business vocabulary accurately throughout.
wider: Create an explanation that integrates both qualitative information (case study, expert commentary) and quantitative data (statistics, trend data) — and analyses what each type of evidence contributes to the explanation

Produce an explanation in a data visualisation format (e.g. an annotated graph, an infographic with supporting text) and evaluate whether the format communicates the issue and evidence more or less effectively than prose

Evaluate an economic explanation produced by someone else (a news article, a student sample) against criteria: Does it orient the audience? Does it use concepts accurately? Does the evidence support the conclusion? Provide written feedback using those criteria

modes.reason: Creating evidence-referenced explanations improves through repeated practice across different issue types and formats. Students benefit from producing explanations of market issues, business strategy issues, and taxation/financial planning issues before formal assessment.

descriptors.title: Australia's financial sector
descriptors.description: the role of Australia's financial sector and its effect on economic decision-making by individuals, businesses and global markets
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8: how markets influence resource allocation decisions and the effect of prices (AC9HE8K01); how businesses adapt to market opportunities and changing work (AC9HE8K02); First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs in markets (AC9HE8K03). Students understand basic market mechanisms and business types but have not yet studied the financial sector's specific role as an intermediary.

nodes.label: Structure of the financial sector
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main types of organisations within Australia's financial sector and describe their core functions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish organisational types from functions will conflate what a financial institution is with what it does, causing persistent confusion when explaining how the sector affects decision-making in subsequent nodes.
criteria: Names at least three types of organisations within Australia's financial sector
Describes the core function of each named organisation type
Distinguishes between types (e.g. bank vs credit union) based on ownership or structure

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of financial organisations (e.g. banks, credit unions) and describe one core function each (e.g. collecting deposits, lending funds).
width.typical: Identify the range of organisations within Australia's financial sector — banks, credit unions, building societies, insurance companies, superannuation funds — and explain their distinct functions including collecting deposits, pooling savings, lending, providing insurance, and managing long-term savings.
wider: Compare the ownership and governance models of mutual organisations (credit unions, building societies) with shareholder-owned banks, examining how structure affects decision-making and consumer outcomes
Investigate the role of non-bank financial institutions (e.g. fintech lenders, buy-now-pay-later providers) and how they have changed the structure of Australia's financial sector
Examine how First Nations Community Development Finance Institutions (CDFIs) provide financial services to underserved communities, comparing their functions with mainstream banks

modes.reason: Use a structured table: institution type → ownership → core function → who it serves. The category-function distinction is non-obvious and benefits from explicit visual scaffolding before moving to effects.
Multiple institution types (banks, credit unions, super funds, insurance companies) in different contexts help students see that the sector is a system of specialised roles, not just 'banks'.

nodes.label: Financial products and investment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what investment means and describe how financial products enable individuals to receive future income.
criteria: Explains what investment means (committing funds to receive future income)
Describes how at least two named financial products generate returns for investors
Uses correct economic terminology (e.g. returns, interest, dividends, capital growth)

width.minimum: Explain the concept of investment using one financial product (e.g. shares or term deposits) to show how it generates future income.
width.typical: Explain the nature of investment — committing funds now to receive income in the future — and describe how a range of financial products serve this purpose: shares (dividends, capital growth), term deposits (interest), managed funds (pooled investment), and superannuation (retirement income). Explain how each product generates returns.
wider: Investigate how superannuation functions as Australia's mandatory retirement saving system, examining how fund choice and investment strategy affect long-term outcomes for individuals
Compare traditional investment products with newer platforms (e.g. micro-investing apps, ETFs) and explain what has changed about how Australians access investment
Examine ethical investment funds and ESG criteria, exploring how values-based investing has created new product categories and changed investment decision-making

modes.reason: Students need a repertoire of product types to address the range of elaboration examples. Building this incrementally — one product at a time — before comparing them is more effective than presenting all at once.

nodes.label: Debt, savings and financial management
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between good and bad debt, describe how to manage debt, and explain why a savings buffer matters.
nodes.hinge_reason: The good/bad debt distinction is a prerequisite for understanding how the financial sector affects decision-making — students who cannot distinguish productive from unproductive debt cannot analyse the effects of lending practices or consumer financial decisions in subsequent nodes.
criteria: Distinguishes good debt from bad debt with reference to purpose and financial outcome
Identifies at least two risks associated with over-indebtedness
Explains why maintaining a savings buffer reduces financial risk

width.minimum: Distinguish good debt (used to build assets or income) from bad debt (consumer debt with high interest) and explain one risk of over-indebtedness.
width.typical: Explain the difference between good and bad debt (purpose, interest cost, asset or liability creation), describe strategies for managing debt (budgeting, prioritising repayment, avoiding compound interest traps), explain the risks of over-indebtedness (financial stress, restricted economic decision-making), and explain why a savings buffer provides financial security.
wider: Analyse the growth of buy-now-pay-later services in Australia and evaluate whether they represent a new category of consumer debt risk for young people
Examine how student loan debt (HECS-HELP) differs from commercial debt in its interest treatment and repayment structure, and explain why this matters for young Australians' decision-making
Investigate patterns of household debt in Australia compared with other OECD countries, explaining what these patterns reveal about Australian consumer behaviour and financial vulnerability

modes.reason: The good/bad debt distinction requires students to reason about purpose, cost and outcome simultaneously. A structured decision framework (purpose → interest rate → asset/liability outcome) prevents students from treating 'all debt is bad' as the answer.

nodes.label: Forces shaping Australia's financial landscape
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the forces that shape and affect Australia's financial landscape, including deregulation, technology, economic conditions and consumer sentiment.
criteria: Names at least two forces that shape Australia's financial landscape
Explains how each named force affects the behaviour of financial institutions or their customers
Uses relevant economic terms (e.g. deregulation, sentiment, capital, competition)

width.minimum: Identify and explain one force that has shaped Australia's financial landscape (e.g. financial deregulation or technological change) and describe its effect on financial sector behaviour.
width.typical: Explain the range of forces shaping Australia's financial landscape: financial deregulation (opening competition, reducing barriers), technological change (digital banking, fintech, open banking), economic and business activity cycles (how economic conditions affect lending and investment), and consumer and business sentiment (how confidence affects spending, saving and borrowing). Explain how each force affects the behaviour of financial institutions and their customers.
wider: Investigate Australia's financial deregulation in the 1980s — what changed, which institutions were affected, and how it reshaped competition and consumer access to financial products

Examine how the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry (2018) changed regulation of Australia's financial sector and its effects on consumer protection
Analyse the emergence of open banking in Australia and explain how data-sharing between institutions is changing competitive dynamics and consumer decision-making

modes.reason: Each force (deregulation, technology, cycles, sentiment) represents a distinct explanatory context. Using multiple real Australian examples — the 1980s deregulation, the GFC, the rise of fintechs — prevents students from learning only one causal story.

nodes.label: The financial sector in global markets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how Australia's financial sector supports businesses in global markets, including payment systems, currency access, insurance and capital.
criteria: Identifies at least two services the financial sector provides to businesses operating in global markets
Explains how each named service enables international trade or investment
Connects financial sector services to economic decision-making by businesses

width.minimum: Identify one way Australia's financial sector supports businesses operating in global markets (e.g. currency exchange, payment clearing) and explain why this matters for international trade.
width.typical: Explain how Australia's financial sector supports businesses in global markets across the range of elaboration examples: global financial services (trade finance, letters of credit), payment systems (clearing and settlement of international transactions), access to foreign currencies, international insurance, and access to capital for investment in global operations. Explain how each service enables Australian businesses to participate in global trade.
wider: Examine how correspondent banking relationships connect Australian banks to international payment networks and explain the risks when these relationships are withdrawn (derisking)
Investigate how Australian superannuation funds invest in global markets and explain the effect of this on Australia's financial integration with the global economy
Analyse a case where disruption to global financial systems (e.g. sanctions, correspondent banking withdrawal) affected Australian businesses or individuals, explaining the channels of effect

modes.reason: This node integrates the sector structure (Node 1), financial products (Node 2), and forces shaping the sector (Node 4) into an explanation of how the sector enables global economic participation. Students should connect prior nodes explicitly — the sector's structure enables the services that support global trade.

descriptors.title: Economic interdependence
descriptors.description: how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HE9K01 (direct predecessor): Australia's financial sector — its structure, functions, products and global role. From Y8: market mechanisms and price signals (AC9HE8K01), business adaptation (AC9HE8K02). Students understand how individual actors operate in markets but have not yet analysed how their decisions are mutually dependent within local, national and global economic systems.

nodes.label: The circular flow of economic decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government play interdependent roles in economic decision-making within local, national and global contexts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand each actor in isolation but not interdependence will be unable to analyse how decisions propagate through the system — the core demand of this descriptor and a prerequisite for understanding globalisation effects in subsequent nodes.
criteria: Names all four actors in economic decision-making
Explains, using an example, how a decision by one actor affects at least one other actor
Uses terms such as 'interdependence', 'consumer', 'financial sector' correctly

width.minimum: Describe how two of the four actors (e.g. consumers and businesses) make interdependent decisions, using one concrete example.
width.typical: Explain the interdependent nature of economic decision-making across all four actors — consumers (purchasing goods and services), businesses (organising production and distribution), the financial sector (facilitating investment and credit), and government (setting rules, collecting taxes, providing services) — within local, national and global contexts. Use examples showing how a decision by one actor affects others.
wider: Trace how a change in consumer sentiment (e.g. reduced spending during economic uncertainty) flows through all four actors — affecting business revenue, financial sector lending, and government tax receipts
Compare how the four-actor interdependence operates differently at local (community business), national (ASX-listed firm) and global (transnational corporation) scales
Examine how First Nations community enterprises operate within this interdependence, including distinctive relationships with government and community consumers

modes.reason: The circular flow model requires students to trace decision chains across actors. A visual diagram of actor relationships with explicit arrows showing decision flows helps students reason about interdependence rather than treating actors as independent.
Multiple scale contexts (local, national, global) prevent students from thinking interdependence only operates at one level — a common misconception that limits transfer to globalisation analysis.

nodes.label: Globalisation and supply chains
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how globalisation supports transnational corporations using supply chains, and can describe advantages and disadvantages for businesses, workers and consumers.
criteria: Explains what a supply chain is and how transnational corporations use them
Identifies at least one advantage and one disadvantage of globalised supply chains for a named stakeholder group
Uses terms such as 'globalisation', 'supply chain', 'transnational corporation'

width.minimum: Explain what a supply chain is and identify one advantage and one disadvantage of globalised supply chains for either businesses, workers or consumers.
width.typical: Explain how globalisation enables transnational corporations to use supply chains to develop, produce and deliver products or services across countries. Explain advantages for businesses (cost reduction, market access, specialisation), workers (employment, skill development) and consumers (lower prices, product variety), and disadvantages for each (loss of local manufacturing, labour exploitation, dependency risks, price volatility). Use at least one named example.
wider: Investigate a specific Australian industry (e.g. clothing retail, electronics, agriculture) to trace its global supply chain and identify which advantages and disadvantages are most significant for Australian stakeholders
Examine the disruption to global supply chains during COVID-19 and explain what this revealed about the risks of highly interdependent global production systems
Analyse how ethical consumerism (e.g. Fair Trade, country-of-origin labelling) represents a consumer response to the disadvantages of globalised supply chains

modes.reason: Students need specific named examples of transnational corporations and supply chains to answer 'analyse implications' type tasks. Building a repertoire of 2-3 concrete cases before analysing implications prevents vague generalisations.

nodes.label: Implications of global economic interdependence for Australia
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse implications of interdependence within the global economy for Australian consumers, workers and businesses, including costs and disruption risks.
criteria: Identifies at least two implications of global economic interdependence for Australian actors
Explains the mechanism by which a change in another country's conditions affects Australian consumers, workers or businesses
Distinguishes implications for different stakeholder groups (consumers vs workers vs businesses)

width.minimum: Identify one implication of global economic interdependence for Australian consumers or businesses (e.g. cost effects from overseas regulation changes or supply disruptions).
width.typical: Analyse the implications of global economic interdependence for Australian consumers (product costs, price fluctuations, access to variety), workers (employment in trade-exposed industries, skill demands) and businesses (cost structures, supply reliability, regulatory exposure). Include examples of how changes to regulations, economic conditions or disruptions in another country affect Australian actors.
wider: Investigate how changes to Chinese economic policy or consumer preferences have affected Australian export industries (e.g. iron ore, education, agricultural exports) and trace implications for workers and businesses
Examine how trade sanctions or geopolitical tensions (e.g. trade disputes between major economies) create uncertainty for Australian businesses operating in global markets
Analyse how digital trade and platform economy companies (e.g. streaming services, ride-sharing) have created new forms of global economic interdependence affecting Australian consumers and workers

modes.reason: The implications vary significantly by stakeholder group and industry. Multiple Australian case contexts (manufacturing, agriculture, services, digital economy) prevent students from generalising from one sector to all.

nodes.label: How national economic conditions affect other nations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain, using examples, how changes to one nation's economic conditions affect other nations through interdependent relationships.
criteria: Explains the causal chain by which a change in one nation's economic conditions affects another nation
Uses a named real example to illustrate the explanation
Connects the explanation to effects on Australian consumers, businesses or workers

width.minimum: Using one example, explain how a change in one country's economic condition (e.g. rising unemployment) affects another country's economy (e.g. reduced demand for exports).
width.typical: Explain how changes to a nation's economic conditions — unemployment, interest rates, consumer demand, economic growth — affect other nations through trade and financial interdependence. Use the elaboration example (rising unemployment → reduced consumer demand → lower imports → affected export revenues in other countries) and at least one additional example showing different causal chains. Connect to how Australia is affected by conditions in major trading partners.
wider: Investigate how the Global Financial Crisis (2008) spread from the US financial sector to affect economic conditions in countries with different levels of financial integration, including Australia
Examine how China's economic slowdown periods have created ripple effects in Australia's mining sector, housing market and tertiary education — tracing the causal chain for each
Analyse how a rise in US interest rates affects borrowing costs, currency values and investment decisions in countries with different levels of economic interdependence with the US

modes.reason: This node integrates interdependence (Node 1), supply chains (Node 2), and Australian implications (Node 3) into an explanation of bidirectional cross-national effects. Students should trace the causal chain explicitly: national condition → mechanism → effect on other nations → effect on Australia.

descriptors.title: Australia-Asia trade
descriptors.description: the reasons Australia trades with other nations, and the patterns of trade between Australia and Asia
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HE9K02 (direct predecessor): how economic decision-making involves interdependence of consumers, businesses, financial sector and government, including globalisation and supply chains. From AC9HE9K01: Australia's financial sector and its global role. Students understand economic interdependence but have not yet specifically investigated why countries trade or analysed Australia's trade relationship with Asia.

nodes.label: Why countries trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the reasons countries trade, including resource variations, comparative advantage, surplus goods and specialist goods.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand trade only as 'buying what you can't make' will be unable to analyse Australia's trade patterns in subsequent nodes — many Australian exports (iron ore, coal, education) are sold to countries that could obtain alternatives, making the resource-advantage and surplus explanations essential for accurate pattern analysis.
criteria: Explains at least two distinct reasons why countries trade
Uses a concrete example to illustrate each reason
Uses terms such as 'specialisation', 'comparative advantage', 'resources' correctly

width.minimum: Explain two reasons why countries trade (e.g. variations in resource availability and the ability to sell surplus production).
width.typical: Explain the full range of reasons countries trade: variations in quantity and quality of economic resources within and between countries; ability to sell surplus goods and services; need to buy goods and services not produced domestically; comparative advantage (specialising in what they produce most efficiently). Use concrete examples for each reason.
wider: Examine comparative advantage theory through a concrete bilateral example (e.g. Australia-Japan trade) and explain how specialisation creates mutual benefit even when one country could produce both goods
Investigate how trade agreements (e.g. ASEAN-Australia-NZ FTA, ChAFTA) reduce barriers to trade and explain how they change the reasons and incentives for trading
Analyse how non-economic reasons for trade (diplomatic relationships, national security, cultural exchange) interact with economic reasons in shaping Australia's trade partnerships

modes.reason: Trade reasons are often conflated by students (especially comparative advantage, which is counterintuitive). A structured framework — resource difference → specialisation → mutual benefit — helps students reason about why trade creates gains rather than treating it as a zero-sum exchange.

nodes.label: Benefits of trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the economic, individual, business and national benefits of trade for Australia.
criteria: Identifies benefits of trade from at least two categories (economic, individual/business, national)
Explains each benefit with reference to an Australian example
Distinguishes between different types of trade benefits rather than listing them as equivalent

width.minimum: Identify and explain two benefits of trade — one economic benefit (e.g. increased production or household income) and one national or individual benefit.
width.typical: Explain the full range of trade benefits across the elaboration categories: economic benefits (increased production, specialisation, increased household incomes, increased employment); benefits for individuals and businesses (opportunities to sell surpluses, competition encouraging greater choice, connections for inventors and entrepreneurs with future discoveries); and national benefits (relationships between countries, access to health and education services, diversified sources of national income). Use Australian examples for each category.
wider: Evaluate the distribution of trade benefits within Australia — examining which industries, regions and demographic groups gain most from trade liberalisation and which may be disadvantaged
Investigate how services trade (education, tourism, financial services) creates benefits for Australia that differ in nature from goods trade benefits
Examine how Indigenous-owned businesses in Australia participate in trade (domestic and international) and what barriers or opportunities shape their experience of trade benefits

modes.reason: Students need examples across all three benefit categories (economic, individual/business, national) to address descriptor-level tasks. Systematically building the repertoire with Australian examples before analysis tasks prevents students from relying on one category only.

nodes.label: Patterns of Australia-Asia trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse patterns of trade between Australia and Asian countries over time, including total value, composition and direction of trade.
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysing trade patterns requires being able to read multi-variable data (value, composition, direction, time) simultaneously. Students who cannot disaggregate pattern dimensions cannot address the analytical tasks in AC9HE9S03, which uses Australia-Asia trade as a primary example context.
criteria: Identifies the composition and direction of trade between Australia and at least one Asian country
Describes at least one trend in Australia-Asia trade patterns over time
Uses trade data vocabulary (exports, imports, total value, composition, direction)

width.minimum: Describe the current direction of trade between Australia and one Asian country (what Australia exports and imports) and identify one trend in this relationship over the past decade.
width.typical: Analyse patterns of trade between Australia and the countries of Asia over time using the elaboration dimensions: total value of trade each year; composition of trade (category of goods and services — resources, agricultural products, manufactured goods, services); direction of trade (exports to which countries, imports from which countries); and percentage change over a decade. Identify trends and changes in these patterns.
wider: Compare Australia's trade composition with Asia now versus 50 years ago, explaining what the shifts in composition reveal about changes in comparative advantage and economic development
Investigate the growth of services trade between Australia and Asia (education, tourism, financial services) alongside goods trade, and explain why services have grown as a share of the total

Analyse how China's economic development has changed its role in Australia's trade patterns — from a smaller trading partner to Australia's largest — and explain the economic factors driving this shift

modes.reason: Trade pattern analysis involves multiple simultaneous variables (value, composition, direction, change over time). A structured data-reading framework — what is traded, with whom, how much, how has this changed — prevents students from treating pattern analysis as a single-variable description.

Different Asian trading partners (China, Japan, South Korea, India, ASEAN) show different pattern characteristics. Using multiple partner contexts reveals the variation within 'Australia-Asia trade' and builds more accurate pattern understanding.

nodes.label: Similarities, differences and interdependence in Australia-Asia trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in Australia-Asia trade patterns over time and explain the interdependent nature of this trade relationship.
criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference in Australia-Asia trade patterns across different time periods
Explains how both Australia and Asian trading partners are interdependent in the trade relationship
Connects trade patterns to the underlying economic reasons for the relationship

width.minimum: Identify one similarity and one difference in Australia's trade relationship with Asia now compared with 50 years ago, and explain one way the relationship is interdependent.
width.typical: Identify similarities and differences or trends in the composition and direction of trade between Australia and Asia now and 50 years ago (e.g. what goods/services have remained dominant, what has changed, which partners have risen or fallen in importance). Explain the interdependent nature of Australia-Asia trade — how Australian producers depend on Asian markets and Asian economies depend on Australian resources, commodities and services.
wider: Investigate how Australia's economic dependence on Asian demand for resources creates vulnerability — using a specific commodity and examining the consequences of demand fluctuation for Australian industries and regions
Examine the interdependence between Australian universities and international student income from Asian countries, analysing how COVID-19 border closures exposed this dependency
Analyse how new trade corridors (e.g. India, Vietnam, Indonesia) are diversifying Australia's trade interdependence and explain what is driving these shifts

modes.reason: This node integrates reasons for trade (Node 1), benefits of trade (Node 2), and pattern analysis (Node 3) into an explanation of the Australia-Asia interdependence. Students should connect: why trade exists → what patterns have developed → how these create mutual dependence.

descriptors.title: Competitive advantage
descriptors.description: processes that businesses use to create and maintain competitive advantage, including the role of entrepreneurs
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8: how businesses adapt to market opportunities and the changing nature of work (AC9HE8K02); how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs develop market opportunities (AC9HE8K03). From Y7: entrepreneur characteristics and how these influence business success (AC9HE7K03). Students understand why businesses exist and how entrepreneurs operate but have not yet studied the specific processes used to create and maintain competitive advantage in global markets.

nodes.label: First Nations businesses and competitive advantage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain processes used by First Nations Australian businesses to outperform competitors and innovate in global markets, including managing cultural and intellectual property.
nodes.hinge_reason: The First Nations IP and cultural property management context is substantively different from mainstream competitive advantage processes and must be treated on its own terms before students can make meaningful comparisons. Students who are taught generic competitive advantage first and then receive First Nations content as an 'add-on' develop a distorted understanding of the processes involved.
criteria: Identifies at least two processes First Nations Australian businesses use to create or maintain competitive advantage
Explains how cultural and intellectual property management contributes to competitive advantage for First Nations businesses
Uses relevant terms (e.g. 'competitive advantage', 'intellectual property', 'cultural expression')

width.minimum: Identify one process used by a First Nations Australian business to create competitive advantage (e.g. brand image, cultural IP licensing) and explain how it differentiates the business.
width.typical: Identify and explain the range of processes First Nations Australian businesses use to build competitive advantage: promoting brand image and uniqueness of experiences; managing cultural and intellectual property through copyright and licensing; maintaining, controlling and protecting cultural expressions in products and services (art licensing, music licensing, cultural site consulting); and collaborating through the First Nations Chamber of Commerce and Industry to share resources and build market presence.
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations Australian business operating in global markets and analyse which competitive advantage processes it uses, explaining what makes its approach distinctive
Examine how First Nations cultural intellectual property differs from mainstream IP in Australian law and explain how this shapes the strategies businesses use to protect competitive advantage
Compare how First Nations businesses in different sectors (tourism, food, art, consulting) use different combinations of the identified processes to build competitive advantage

modes.reason: Multiple First Nations business examples across different sectors (art, tourism, food, consulting) show that the IP-protection and branding processes are adapted to different contexts, not a single formula.

nodes.label: Why businesses seek competitive advantage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why businesses seek to build competitive advantage, including meeting changing market demands and improving profit margins.
criteria: Explains at least two reasons why businesses seek competitive advantage
Connects the reasons to conditions in competitive or global markets
Uses terms such as 'profit margin', 'competitive market', 'global market'

width.minimum: Explain two reasons why businesses seek competitive advantage (e.g. to meet competitive market demands, to improve profitability).
width.typical: Explain the reasons businesses seek to build or create competitive advantage: to meet the changing demands of a competitive global market (which shifts preferences, lowers barriers, and creates new entrants); to improve profit margins (by achieving premium prices or reducing costs relative to competitors); to sustain long-term viability in dynamic markets. Connect these reasons to the pressures businesses face in the global economy.
wider: Examine why competitive advantage is harder to sustain in digital markets (e.g. software, media) than in physical goods markets, and explain what this means for how businesses approach advantage-building
Investigate how competitor actions in global supply chains have forced Australian businesses to change their competitive advantage strategies — using a specific industry example
Analyse how shifting consumer values (e.g. sustainability, ethical sourcing) are changing the reasons businesses seek certain types of competitive advantage

modes.reason: Students benefit from reasoning through the competitive pressure logic: market → competitive entry → price/quality pressure → need to differentiate → processes to achieve differentiation. This causal chain makes the 'why' of competitive advantage concrete rather than a list of reasons.

nodes.label: Building connections as a competitive process
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain processes businesses use to build connections that support competitive advantage, including industry collaboration, government partnerships and developing professional talent.
criteria: Identifies at least two types of connection processes businesses use to build competitive advantage
Explains how each connection type creates or maintains advantage
Uses concrete examples of connection processes in Australian contexts

width.minimum: Identify and explain one process businesses use to build connections (e.g. industry cost-sharing, export partnerships with government) and explain how it supports competitive advantage.
width.typical: Explain the processes businesses use to build connections that support competitive advantage: working with other businesses within the industry to share promotion costs and market access; working with government to increase exports (e.g. trade missions, export grants, bilateral agreements); developing highly skilled professionals and leaders across different industries to sustain competitive capability over time. Explain how each connection process creates advantage.
wider: Investigate an Australian industry association or export council and analyse how collective action through these bodies creates competitive advantage that individual businesses could not achieve alone
