Examine how Australian universities and research institutions partner with businesses to develop human capital, and explain how this contributes to long-term competitive advantage in knowledge-intensive industries
Analyse how government-backed trade promotion programs (e.g. Austrade) support Australian businesses in building international connections, including evaluation of their effectiveness

modes.reason: Each connection type (industry, government, talent development) requires separate examples. Building a repertoire of specific Australian programs and partnerships — rather than treating connections generically — prepares students for evidence-based analysis tasks.

nodes.label: Cost reduction and innovation processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the processes businesses use to produce goods and services at lower cost and to innovate and differentiate products and services from competitors.
criteria: Explains at least one process businesses use to reduce production costs
Explains at least one process businesses use to differentiate products or services from competitors
Connects each process to competitive advantage using correct economic terminology

width.minimum: Explain one process a business uses to reduce production costs (e.g. R&D, outsourcing) and one process used to differentiate products from competitors (e.g. advertising, unique attributes).
width.typical: Explain the processes businesses use to produce goods and services at lower cost: research and development to improve efficiency; improving efficiency in development, production or delivery processes; utilising local resources; and outsourcing labour in the global economy. Explain the processes businesses use to innovate and differentiate: developing identifiable marketable attributes; using advertising and social media to build brand recognition and customer loyalty. Connect each process to how it creates or maintains competitive advantage.
wider: Investigate how a specific Australian business uses R&D investment to create competitive advantage — examining what it invests in, what outcomes it achieves, and how this compares to international competitors
Examine the ethical implications of using outsourced labour in global supply chains for competitive advantage — considering impacts on workers, communities and the business's reputation

Analyse how social media has changed the cost of differentiation for small businesses, and compare how a First Nations small business uses social media for competitive differentiation versus a multinational corporation

modes.reason: This node integrates all prior competitive advantage processes — First Nations approaches (Node 1), reasons for seeking advantage (Node 2), and connection-building (Node 3) — into a full picture of how businesses create and maintain advantage. Students should see cost reduction and innovation as additions to the toolkit, not replacements for earlier processes.

Cost reduction and innovation operate very differently across sectors (manufacturing vs services vs digital). Multiple sector examples prevent students from applying a manufacturing-only mental model to all businesses.

descriptors.title: Consumer and financial risk
descriptors.description: how individuals and businesses manage consumer and financial risks and rewards
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 (direct predecessor AC9HE8K05): processes individuals and businesses use to plan and budget to achieve short- and long-term financial objectives. From Y7 (AC9HE7K05): consumer rights and responsibilities of individuals and businesses relating to financial products and services. Students understand planning, budgeting and consumer rights but have not yet studied active risk management strategies — the move from understanding what rights exist to understanding how to manage active threats.

nodes.label: Types of consumer and financial risk
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and discuss examples of consumer and financial risk to individuals and businesses, including scams, identity theft and fraudulent transactions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish between risk types will be unable to match appropriate management strategies to specific risks in subsequent nodes — applying insurance to a scam, for example, is not meaningful risk management and reflects category confusion.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of consumer or financial risk
Describes how each risk type affects individuals or businesses
Distinguishes between risk types rather than treating them as equivalent

width.minimum: Identify and describe two types of consumer or financial risk (e.g. scams, identity theft) and explain how each affects individuals or businesses.
width.typical: Identify and discuss the range of consumer and financial risks to individuals and businesses from the elaboration examples: scams (phishing, investment scams, social engineering), identity theft (unauthorised use of personal information for financial gain), and fraudulent transactions (unauthorised payments, card fraud). Explain how each type affects individuals and businesses differently in terms of financial loss, reputational damage and emotional harm.
wider: Investigate current scam types targeting Australian consumers and businesses (using ACCC Scamwatch data) and analyse which demographic groups are most affected and why
Examine how cybersecurity incidents in businesses create consumer financial risk — using a real Australian data breach case to trace consequences for both the business and affected customers
Analyse how social media and digital platforms have created new categories of consumer and financial risk that did not exist a decade ago

modes.reason: Risk categories (scams, identity theft, fraud) each have distinct mechanisms. Building a repertoire of current, realistic examples from Australian contexts — not abstract definitions — makes the subsequent strategy-matching work genuine.

nodes.label: Consumer reward programs and financial rewards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss examples of consumer reward programs and financial rewards, including loyalty schemes and investment returns.
criteria: Describes at least two types of consumer or financial reward with examples
Explains how each reward mechanism functions
Uses terms such as 'loyalty scheme', 'investment returns', 'savings'

width.minimum: Describe one consumer reward program and one type of financial reward (e.g. investment return) and explain how each benefits individuals or businesses.
width.typical: Discuss examples of consumer rewards from the elaboration range: innovative products and services that reward early adopters; benefits accrued through loyalty schemes (frequent flyer points, cashback, member discounts); and rewards for building savings and making investments (interest on term deposits, dividends from shares, capital growth from home ownership). Explain how each rewards mechanism functions and who benefits.
wider: Investigate the economics of loyalty programs — examining how businesses profit from them while appearing to reward consumers — and evaluate whether loyalty programs are genuinely beneficial for consumers or primarily for businesses
Examine how the rewards from home ownership vary across income levels and geographic locations in Australia, and discuss what this reveals about equity in financial reward distribution
Compare investment rewards available to young Australians (micro-investing, superannuation, first home saver accounts) and analyse which reward mechanisms are most accessible

modes.reason: Reward mechanisms differ significantly across loyalty programs, savings products and investment assets. Multiple examples prevent students from conflating reward types and support a balanced risk-reward discussion in the final node.

nodes.label: Individual strategies to manage consumer and financial risk
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain strategies individuals use to manage consumer and financial risk, including goal-setting, insurance, savings and scam alertness.
criteria: Identifies at least two strategies individuals use to manage consumer or financial risk
Explains the mechanism by which each strategy reduces exposure to risk
Matches strategies to appropriate risk types

width.minimum: Identify and explain two strategies individuals use to manage consumer or financial risk (e.g. maintaining a savings buffer, checking for scams before engaging).
width.typical: Identify and explain the range of strategies individuals use to manage consumer and financial risk from the elaboration examples: setting financial goals (having a plan reduces impulsive decisions and builds resilience); maintaining insurance (transfers risk of major losses); building savings (provides a buffer against unexpected financial shocks); and being alert to scams (recognising warning signs, verifying contacts, using official channels). Explain how each strategy reduces exposure to specific risks.
wider: Investigate how financial literacy levels in Australia vary by demographic group and analyse how this affects individuals' capacity to implement risk management strategies
Examine the role of government consumer protection resources (e.g. ASIC's MoneySmart, ACCC Scamwatch) in supporting individual risk management — evaluating whether they are effective

Analyse a case where an individual failed to use available risk management strategies and experienced significant consumer or financial harm — identifying which strategies, if applied, would have reduced the risk

modes.reason: Strategy-to-risk matching requires systematic reasoning: risk type → strategy that addresses it → mechanism by which the strategy reduces exposure. Without this structure, students list strategies without connecting them to specific risks.

nodes.label: Business practices for consumer protection and ethical decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify business practices that protect consumer safety and reflect on the importance of ethical decision-making and corporate social responsibility in consumer and financial contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least two business practices that protect consumer safety
Explains why ethical decision-making and CSR are important in consumer and financial contexts
Considers consequences for multiple stakeholders (individuals, community, environment)

width.minimum: Identify one practice businesses use to protect consumer safety (e.g. mandatory product standards, cooling-off periods) and explain why ethical decision-making matters for consumers and businesses.
width.typical: Identify and explain practices businesses use to protect consumer safety: mandatory and voluntary standards (product safety requirements), product safety recalls (removing dangerous products from market), and cooling-off periods (allowing consumers to reverse financial decisions). Reflect on the importance of ethical decision-making and corporate social responsibility when making consumer and financial decisions — including consequences for customers, families, communities and the environment.
wider: Investigate a specific Australian product recall or consumer protection enforcement action and analyse what the business did, what it should have done, and the consequences of its actions for consumers and its own reputation

Examine how corporate social responsibility reporting has changed expectations of business ethical behaviour in Australia, and whether voluntary CSR commitments effectively protect consumers or whether mandatory standards are needed

Analyse how Indigenous consumer protection issues (e.g. predatory financial products targeting remote communities) reveal gaps in Australia's consumer protection system and what businesses and government should do differently

modes.reason: This node integrates risk types (Node 1), rewards (Node 2), and individual strategies (Node 3) into an account of how businesses manage the risk-reward relationship on behalf of consumers. Students should connect: what risks exist → what rewards are offered → how businesses protect consumers from harm while offering rewards.

Ethical decision-making requires students to reason about consequences across multiple stakeholders simultaneously. A stakeholder consequence framework (individual consumer → family → community → environment) structures the reflection so students move beyond 'ethics is good' generalisations.

descriptors.title: Develop and modify inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop and modify questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S01 (direct predecessor): develop questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue. Students can develop questions at Y8 level. Y9 adds two moves: (1) modifying questions to improve focus, and (2) operating with more complex, contemporary issues involving global markets, interdependence and globalisation. The 'modify' move is new and requires meta-cognitive reflection on question quality.

nodes.label: Developing questions for complex economic issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions to investigate a complex contemporary economic and business issue, using economic and business concepts and terms.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot frame questions at the right scope — specific enough to be investigable, broad enough to address the issue's complexity — will not be able to conduct meaningful inquiry. Poor questions at this stage mean all subsequent research, analysis and communication work is anchored to an inadequate inquiry frame.
criteria: Develops at least two questions that use economic and business concepts or terms
Questions are investigable — they can be answered through research into economic and business data or information
Questions address the complexity of a contemporary economic or business issue

width.minimum: Develop at least two questions using economic and business concepts that could guide an investigation of a named contemporary issue.
width.typical: Develop questions that investigate a complex contemporary economic and business issue — using the elaboration examples as models (e.g. 'How do participants in the global economy interact?', 'Why does international trade benefit Australian society?', 'How do businesses create and maintain a competitive advantage?'). Questions should be framed using relevant economic and business concepts and terms (interdependence, trade, competitive advantage, globalisation), be investigable (answerable through research), and be appropriately scoped for the issue's complexity.
wider: Develop questions for a multi-stakeholder issue (e.g. a trade dispute affecting Australian businesses, workers and consumers simultaneously) and explain what makes each question investigable
Develop questions that span multiple scales of analysis (local, national, global) for the same economic issue, and explain how the scale changes what evidence would be needed
Develop questions for a First Nations economic and business context (e.g. land rights and resource royalties, cultural IP and global markets) using appropriate terminology

modes.reason: Question quality requires explicit criteria: Is it investigable? Does it use appropriate concepts? Is it scoped to the issue's complexity? Teaching students to evaluate their own questions against criteria before committing to an investigation frame addresses the cascade risk.

nodes.label: Modifying questions to improve focus
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the focus and scope of an inquiry question and modify it to improve its usefulness for investigating an economic or business issue.
criteria: Modifies at least one inquiry question and explains what was improved by the modification
The modified question is more focused, better scoped, or uses more precise economic terminology than the original
The modification does not introduce a new tangent — it sharpens the original question's focus

width.minimum: Take an existing inquiry question and modify it to improve its focus — explaining what was weak about the original and how the modification improves it.
width.typical: Develop and modify questions to improve the focus of an investigation using economic and business concepts and terms. Apply the elaboration examples as models: narrowing a broad question ('How can consumers protect themselves from risk?' → 'What strategies do Australian consumers use to manage scam risk?'), improving terminology precision, adjusting scope to match available evidence, and checking that modified questions genuinely advance the investigation rather than introducing a new tangent.
wider: Practise question modification through a structured peer feedback cycle — develop a question, receive structured critique on its focus and concept use, modify and re-evaluate
Apply modification to questions across different issue types (trade, consumer protection, competitive advantage) to develop transferable question-quality judgement
Evaluate a set of provided questions of varying quality for the same economic issue and rank them with justification — explaining what makes the best question better than the weaker ones

modes.reason: The modification move requires repeated practice with explicit feedback before it becomes reliable. Students tend to 'modify' by making questions longer rather than sharper. Practise-and-refine cycles with explicit criteria build the precision needed.

Practising modification across different economic issue contexts — trade, consumer risk, competitive advantage — builds transferable question-quality judgement rather than issue-specific question templates.

descriptors.title: Locate, select and analyse sources
descriptors.description: locate, select and analyse information and data from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S02 (direct predecessor): locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources. Students can locate and organise sources. Y9 adds 'analyse' to the capability — specifically analysing for relevance (does this help answer the question?) and reliability (who collected it, when, why?) — and adds selecting and presenting data using specialised digital tools and processes.

nodes.label: Locating sources using contextually specific search strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate online sources using contextually specific economic and business terms and criteria relevant to the issue being investigated.
criteria: Uses specific economic and business search terms or criteria to locate sources
Identifies at least two sources relevant to the investigation issue
Explains why each located source is likely to contain relevant evidence

width.minimum: Locate at least two relevant sources using specific economic and business search terms (not generic terms) for a nominated issue.
width.typical: Locate online sources using contextually specific terms (e.g. 'global markets', 'trade between Australia and Asia', 'consumer scam risk') or criteria (e.g. 'find case studies related to trade between Australia and Asia'). Demonstrate that search strategies are tailored to the issue's economic and business context rather than generic, and that the search approach identifies sources with the type of evidence needed to address the inquiry question.
wider: Apply structured search strategies across different source types — official government statistics (ABS, RBA), industry reports, academic summaries, news sources — and explain why each type is appropriate for different evidence needs

Locate sources for a contested economic issue (e.g. effects of trade liberalisation) from multiple perspectives — government, business peak bodies, consumer advocates — and document the search process

Use specialist economic databases or tools (e.g. World Bank Open Data, DFAT trade statistics portal, ABS.Stat) to locate primary statistical data and explain when primary data is preferable to secondary commentary

modes.reason: Students benefit from a repertoire of specific source types and databases for Economics and Business investigations. Introducing each source type with a demonstration of its strengths — and when to prefer it — builds search capability beyond 'Google it'.

nodes.label: Selecting for relevance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select information and data from sources by asking and applying questions about relevance to their economic or business investigation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot discriminate between relevant and irrelevant sources will produce investigations crowded with loosely related information. This blocks meaningful analysis in AC9HE9S03 and undermines the quality of arguments in AC9HE9S05.
criteria: Applies at least one explicit relevance criterion to evaluate a source
Explains how selected information helps answer a specific economic or business question
Distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant information from the same source

width.minimum: Apply at least one relevance criterion (e.g. 'Does this data help answer my question?') to select information from a provided source, explaining the selection decision.
width.typical: Select and analyse information and data for relevance by applying the elaboration questions: 'How will the data or information help answer this economic or business question?' and 'How will the data or information inform a response to an economic or business issue?' Apply these criteria to select from a range of sources for a specific investigation, explaining selection and rejection decisions explicitly.
wider: Apply relevance selection across sources of varying types (statistical data, case study, policy document, news report) for the same investigation, explaining how relevance criteria apply differently to each type
Practise the 'relevance decision' under conditions of abundance — given 8-10 possible sources, narrow to 3-4 and justify each inclusion and exclusion with specific relevance reasoning
Apply relevance criteria to a First Nations economic context — locating and selecting sources that are relevant to, and respectful of, community-specific economic and business issues

modes.reason: Relevance requires explicit reasoning against the inquiry question — it is not a 'feels relevant' judgement. Teaching students to articulate the connection (this data shows X, which addresses Y in my question) prevents acceptance of superficially related sources.

nodes.label: Selecting for reliability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select information and data by evaluating reliability — considering how and when data was collected, who collected it, and for what purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate reliability will use industry-funded or advocacy data as equivalent to peer-reviewed or official statistics, leading to invalid conclusions in analysis tasks and weak justification in evaluative responses.
criteria: Applies at least two reliability criteria (who, when, purpose) to evaluate a source
Explains how reliability judgements affect how a source should be used in an investigation
Distinguishes between sources with different reliability profiles for the same topic

width.minimum: Apply at least two reliability questions (who collected it? when? for what purpose?) to evaluate one source, explaining how the answers affect how the source should be used.
width.typical: Select and analyse information and data for reliability using the elaboration questions: 'How and when was it collected?', 'Who collected the data?', and 'For what purpose was the data collected?' Apply these criteria to assess the reliability of different source types — official statistics, industry-funded reports, advocacy group data, news articles — and explain how reliability judgements affect how sources can be used in an investigation.
wider: Apply reliability analysis to a pair of sources on the same economic issue that reach different conclusions — explaining what the reliability differences reveal about why the conclusions differ

Examine how economic data published by government agencies (ABS, RBA, Treasury) differs in reliability characteristics from data published by industry peak bodies or lobby groups, and explain when each is appropriate to use
Investigate a specific case of misleading economic statistics in Australian public debate — tracing how data collection methods, purpose or framing affected the reliability of claims made

modes.reason: Reliability judgement requires applying multiple criteria simultaneously (when, who, why) and drawing a reasoned conclusion about trustworthiness. A structured evaluation framework prevents students from treating reliability as binary (reliable/not reliable) rather than as a spectrum with specific limitations.

Different source types (official statistics, industry data, advocacy reports) have systematically different reliability profiles. Encountering each type in context — rather than learning reliability as an abstract concept — builds transferable evaluation skill.

nodes.label: Presenting data using digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and present data in appropriate formats using specialised digital tools and processes.
criteria: Selects a presentation format appropriate for the data type and investigation purpose
Produces a correctly labelled table or graph using a digital tool
The presentation makes the relevant pattern or comparison visible without distortion

width.minimum: Select appropriate data from a source and present it in one digital format (e.g. a table or graph) that is appropriate for the data type and investigation purpose.
width.typical: Select and present data in appropriate formats using specialised digital tools and processes — applying the elaboration example (a table and graph showing composition and direction of trade between Australia and Asia). Match data type to presentation format: statistical trends → line graphs; comparisons → bar charts; proportions → pie or stacked charts; multi-variable relationships → tables or scatter plots. Use digital tools to produce clear, correctly labelled visualisations that support the investigation.
wider: Create comparative visualisations from two data sources on the same topic, explaining how the choice of format affects what patterns are visible and which insights are foregrounded
Apply data presentation to a full investigation output — selecting, presenting and annotating multiple data representations that together build an argument about an economic issue
Use open-data tools (e.g. World Bank data visualiser, ABS data explorer) to construct original visualisations rather than reproducing pre-made charts

modes.reason: Data presentation requires repeated practice with feedback to build format-to-data-type matching fluency. Students commonly apply familiar formats (bar charts for everything) without considering whether the format serves the data. Targeted practice with deliberate format choices builds precision.

descriptors.title: Interpret data and make predictions
descriptors.description: interpret information and data, explaining economic and business issues, trends and economic cause-and-effect relationships, and make predictions about consumer and financial impacts
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S03 (direct predecessor): interpret information and data to identify economic and business issues, trends and economic cause-and-effect relationships. Y9 extends the capability in two key directions: (1) explaining rather than merely identifying (the move to explicit explanation of relationships and mechanisms); and (2) making predictions about consumer and financial impacts — a new move requiring projection from trends to future outcomes.

nodes.label: Interpreting to explain economic issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret information to explain the nature and extent of economic and business issues, including how Australian businesses operate in the global economy.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat interpretation as identification ('the issue is X') will not produce the causal explanations required by subsequent nodes or by AC9HE9S05. The explain-not-identify distinction is the primary cognitive advance from Y8, and it must be established before prediction work begins.
criteria: Interprets a source to explain what a named economic or business issue involves
Explains how the issue operates — naming the mechanism or actors driving it
Goes beyond identification to provide an explanation of the issue's nature

width.minimum: Interpret one source (text or data) to explain the nature of a named economic issue — going beyond identifying the issue to explaining what it involves and how it operates.
width.typical: Interpret information to explain the nature and extent of economic and business issues — applying the elaboration example (the way Australian businesses operate in the global economy). Explain what the issue involves (its components and actors), how it operates (the mechanisms at work), and its extent (how widespread or significant it is). Use the source explicitly to support each element of the explanation.
wider: Interpret information from multiple source types (statistical data + case study + expert commentary) to build a richer explanation of the same issue, identifying what each source type adds
Apply the nature-and-extent interpretation framework to a First Nations economic issue, explaining what makes this context require different framing assumptions
Interpret a contested economic issue where sources frame the nature differently (e.g. trade liberalisation as opportunity vs risk) and explain how framing affects the account of 'nature and extent'

modes.reason: The nature-extent explanation framework (what it involves → how it operates → how significant it is) scaffolds interpretation as a three-part explanatory act rather than a description. Making this structure explicit prevents students from treating interpretation as description.

nodes.label: Interpreting multi-variable data for trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret multi-variable data to explain direction and time period for a change, including changes in Australia's trade patterns.
nodes.hinge_reason: Multi-variable trend interpretation is required for AC9HE9K03 (trade patterns) and for prediction tasks in Node 4. Students who can only read single-variable trends cannot perform the combined-pattern reading that makes trade data analysis meaningful.
criteria: Identifies at least two variables in a multi-variable data source
Explains the direction and time period of change for each variable
Describes what the combined pattern of change reveals about the economic issue

width.minimum: Interpret a graph or table showing change over time to explain the direction and time period of one change.
width.typical: Interpret multi-variable data to explain direction and time period for change — applying the elaboration example (change in direction and composition of Australia's trade over 10, 20 or 50 years). For multi-variable data: identify what variables are shown, describe the direction of change for each (increase, decrease, stable, fluctuating), identify the time period, and explain what the combined pattern reveals about the underlying economic issue.
wider: Compare trend interpretations from graphs using different time scales (10-year vs 50-year) for the same data, explaining how time scale affects which trends are visible

Interpret trade data showing multiple simultaneous trends (total value increasing, composition shifting, direction changing) and explain what the combined picture reveals that single-variable reading would miss
Identify a misleading data visualisation in an economic or business context and explain specifically what is misleading about the trend it appears to show

modes.reason: Multi-variable data interpretation requires a systematic reading sequence: what variables → what direction each → what time period → what the combined pattern means. Without this structure, students read the most visually prominent trend and miss the others.

Practising multi-variable interpretation across different data contexts (trade data, scam loss statistics, unemployment rates) builds transferable data-reading skill rather than context-specific familiarity.

nodes.label: Explaining cause-and-effect relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain cause-and-effect relationships between the actions of individuals and businesses, and between economic actors in different contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least two actors in a cause-and-effect relationship
Traces the mechanism by which one actor's action affects another
Uses source evidence to support each element of the causal explanation

width.minimum: Explain one cause-and-effect relationship between the actions of two economic actors, using evidence from a source.
width.typical: Explain relationships between the actions of individuals and businesses — applying the elaboration example (the way businesses operate in the global economy and implications for the Australian market). For each relationship: identify the actors, describe the action that initiates the chain, trace the effect through intermediate steps, and name the actor(s) affected. Use sources explicitly to support each step of the causal chain.
wider: Trace multi-step causal chains where an initial action triggers sequential effects across multiple actors (e.g. Australian interest rate rise → reduced business borrowing → reduced investment → reduced employment → reduced consumer spending)
Analyse a causal relationship that operates differently across economic scales (local vs global) for the same actors — explaining what changes the mechanism at each scale
Examine a case where a predicted causal relationship did not produce the expected effect and explain what intervening factors disrupted the causal chain

modes.reason: Cause-and-effect explanation requires tracing chains, not just naming pairs. A multi-step chain template (cause → intermediate mechanism → effect on named actor) prevents students from treating 'A affects B' as a sufficient causal explanation.

nodes.label: Making predictions about consumer and financial impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain trends and make predictions about who will be affected and how, including in consumer and financial contexts.
criteria: Identifies a trend and makes a specific, grounded prediction about who will be affected
Explains the mechanism connecting the trend to the predicted impact
The prediction is based on the trend data rather than general opinion or speculation

width.minimum: Use a trend from a data source to make one prediction about who will be affected and how, explaining the reasoning from trend to prediction.
width.typical: Explain trends to make predictions about who will be affected and how — applying the elaboration examples (trend for money lost in scams and age groups most affected; predictions about how it will affect behaviour of individuals and businesses). For each prediction: identify the trend, name the group(s) most likely to be affected, explain the mechanism connecting trend to predicted impact, and state the predicted behavioural or financial change. Predictions should be grounded in the trend data, not speculative.
wider: Make competing predictions from the same trend data by varying assumptions about how actors will respond — explaining what different responses by individuals vs businesses might produce different outcomes
Evaluate the quality of an economic prediction made previously (e.g. from a report 5 years ago) against what actually happened, analysing what the prediction got right, wrong, and why

Apply prediction-making to a First Nations economic context — identifying a trend relevant to First Nations communities and making a grounded prediction about impacts, acknowledging the specific factors that shape outcomes in this context

modes.reason: Prediction integrates trend interpretation (Node 2), causal reasoning (Node 3), and explanatory framing (Node 1). Students should build predictions by: reading the trend → reasoning through the causal mechanism → naming who is affected → predicting the specific impact. This is the full capability the descriptor demands.

Prediction-from-trend is often performed as guessing. A structured prediction argument (trend → mechanism → affected group → predicted change → caveats) helps students produce defensible rather than speculative predictions.

descriptors.title: Evaluate responses to issues
descriptors.description: develop and evaluate a response to an economic and business issue, using cost-benefit analysis or criteria to decide on a course of action
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S04 (direct predecessor): develop a response to an economic and business issue, identifying potential costs and benefits. Students can develop a response with costs and benefits identified. Y9 adds two moves: (1) evaluating the response — not just developing it — and (2) using cost-benefit analysis or explicit criteria to decide on a course of action. The 'evaluate' and 'decide' moves are both new additions to the Y8 capability.

nodes.label: Applying cost-benefit analysis to consumer and financial decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply cost-benefit analysis to consumer and financial decision-making, including estimating costs and considering ability to pay.
nodes.hinge_reason: Cost-benefit analysis is the analytical method underpinning decision justification in this descriptor. Students who treat CBA as 'list good and bad things' rather than as a structured comparative analysis cannot produce the 'justify using criteria' outputs required in later nodes or in AC9HE9S05 arguments.
criteria: Estimates costs (short-term and long-term) for at least two options in a decision
Identifies the benefits associated with each option
Compares options using the cost-benefit analysis and explains which option it supports

width.minimum: Apply cost-benefit analysis to one consumer or financial decision — estimating monthly and annual costs and comparing them against identified benefits.
width.typical: Apply strategies to mitigate risk in consumer and financial decision-making using cost-benefit analysis — applying the elaboration example (estimating monthly and annual costs of each option and considering ability to pay). For each option: estimate short-term and long-term costs; identify direct and indirect benefits; assess affordability (ability to pay without financial stress); and explain which option the analysis supports and why.
wider: Apply cost-benefit analysis to a financial decision that affects multiple household members (e.g. taking on a mortgage vs continuing to rent) — identifying costs and benefits from each member's perspective and explaining how the decision is made when perspectives differ

Apply cost-benefit analysis to a business decision where some costs and benefits are quantifiable and others are not (e.g. reputational benefit, environmental cost) — explaining how non-quantifiable factors should be weighted
Compare how cost-benefit analysis would be conducted differently for a First Nations community enterprise versus a privately-owned business, given different goals and community obligations

modes.reason: CBA requires a structured protocol: identify options → estimate costs (short and long term) → identify benefits → assess affordability → compare and justify. Without this structure, students produce unstructured pros-and-cons lists rather than analysis that can be used to justify a decision.

nodes.label: Opportunity cost in business decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why businesses must consider opportunity cost when deciding on a course of action, using relevant examples.
criteria: Explains what opportunity cost means in a business decision context
Identifies what is foregone in a specific business decision
Uses the term 'opportunity cost' correctly in explaining a business decision

width.minimum: Explain opportunity cost in a business decision context — identifying what is foregone when a business chooses one course of action over another.
width.typical: Examine why businesses must consider opportunity cost when deciding on a course of action — applying the elaboration example (an Australian bank prioritising support for an existing business operating in local and global markets over a new or emerging business). Explain what opportunity cost means in this context: the value of the next-best alternative foregone. Apply this reasoning to at least two business decision contexts.
wider: Examine a real Australian business decision where opportunity cost was significant — tracing what was chosen, what was foregone, and evaluating in retrospect whether the decision was well-made

Apply opportunity cost reasoning to a government resource-allocation decision (e.g. funding one regional infrastructure project over another) and explain why opportunity cost reasoning is more complex for governments than for businesses

Compare how opportunity cost is perceived differently by small businesses versus large corporations — explaining how scale, risk appetite and stakeholder pressures affect opportunity cost calculations

modes.reason: Opportunity cost is frequently misunderstood as 'what you lost' rather than 'the value of the best alternative foregone'. Explicit reasoning through the decision tree — option chosen → options available → best alternative → value of that alternative → opportunity cost — prevents common misconceptions.

nodes.label: Developing response processes using CBA results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop processes that incorporate the results of a cost-benefit analysis to formulate a response to an economic or business issue.
criteria: Develops at least one process that is grounded in a cost-benefit analysis
Explains how the CBA results support the proposed process
The process includes specific steps, not just a general recommendation

width.minimum: Use the results of a cost-benefit analysis to recommend one process a business could use to remain competitive or address an issue, explaining how the CBA supports the recommendation.
width.typical: Develop processes that consider the results of a cost-benefit analysis — applying the elaboration example (processes used by businesses to remain competitive in the global market). Show how CBA outputs (which option has higher net benefit) translate into actionable processes: what steps the business should take, in what sequence, and why. The process should be grounded in the CBA findings, not generic recommendations.
wider: Develop competing response processes for the same business issue from different stakeholder perspectives (e.g. management cost-minimisation process vs worker welfare process) and compare what each CBA prioritises
Apply the process-from-CBA approach to a consumer decision context — developing a decision-making process for managing a specific financial risk that incorporates CBA reasoning at each step
Develop a response process for a complex multi-stakeholder issue (e.g. a business deciding whether to exit a global market) where different actors' CBA results point in different directions

modes.reason: The connection between CBA findings and actionable processes is easier to see in multiple contexts. Business competitiveness, consumer financial risk, and government resource allocation all require this connection but the process steps look different in each context.

nodes.label: Selecting and justifying a preferred response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select a preferred response to an economic or business issue and justify it using criteria such as consumer and financial risk considerations.
criteria: Names at least one criterion used to justify the preferred response
Applies the criterion explicitly to the available options
Explains why the preferred response performs better against the criterion than alternatives

width.minimum: Select one response option and justify it using at least one named criterion (e.g. consumer risk, financial cost, feasibility).
width.typical: Select and justify a preferred response using criteria — applying the elaboration example (criteria such as consideration of consumer and financial risk). For the justification: name the criteria used; explain why these criteria are appropriate for this issue; apply each criterion to the available options; and explain why the preferred response performs better against the criteria than the alternatives. The justification should be explicit about the criteria-to-decision reasoning.
wider: Evaluate two competing responses to the same issue using different criteria sets — explaining how the choice of criteria affects which response is preferred, and discussing what this reveals about whose interests different criteria serve

Apply multi-criteria evaluation to a policy issue (e.g. a trade agreement or consumer protection regulation) from both business and consumer perspectives, explaining where the preferred responses diverge and why

Justify a preferred response to a First Nations economic issue using criteria that include community wellbeing, cultural continuity and sovereignty alongside conventional economic criteria — explaining how this changes the justification

modes.reason: This node integrates CBA (Node 1), opportunity cost (Node 2), and process development (Node 3) into a complete evaluative response. Students should trace: issue → CBA of options → opportunity cost of choices → process recommendation → criteria-based justification of preferred response.

Criteria-based justification requires students to be explicit about the criteria, apply them systematically to each option, and explain the comparative verdict. Without this structure, justifications default to assertion ('I chose X because it is better').

descriptors.title: Create descriptions, explanations and arguments
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings
descriptors.knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S05 (direct predecessor): create descriptions and explanations using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, referencing information and data from sources. Students can create descriptions and explanations with source references. Y9 adds two moves: (1) arguments — a new text type requiring a reasoned position with evidence; and (2) acknowledge research findings — moving from referencing to formal acknowledgement of sources. Y9 also adds audience orientation and appropriate tone.

nodes.label: Orientating the audience using concepts and terms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop responses that orient the audience to an economic or business issue using relevant concepts and terms.
nodes.hinge_reason: Audience orientation determines whether the subsequent explanation and argument are accessible to the reader. A response that fails to orient the audience creates a comprehension gap that undermines the force of the argument regardless of its technical accuracy.
criteria: Identifies the target audience explicitly or through audience-appropriate vocabulary choices
Uses at least two relevant economic or business terms or concepts in the orientation
The orientation establishes what the issue is and why it matters to the specified audience

width.minimum: Write an opening section for an economic or business response that orients a specified audience to the issue using at least two relevant economic or business terms or concepts.
width.typical: Develop a response to an issue that orients the audience (peers or business representatives) using relevant economic and business terms and concepts from the elaboration list: interdependence, trade, comparative advantage, competitive advantage, globalisation, supply chain, financial risks and rewards, return on investment, debt, savings buffer, scams, financial landscape, corporate social responsibility, financial planning, insurance. The orientation should establish what the issue is, why it matters to the audience, and the key concepts that frame the analysis.
wider: Write audience-oriented openings for the same economic issue for two different audiences (e.g. peers and business representatives) — demonstrating how vocabulary, assumed knowledge and framing shift between audiences
Evaluate a provided economic response opening and revise it to better orient a specific audience — explaining each revision decision
Write an orientation to a First Nations economic issue that appropriately contextualises the issue for a non-specialist audience without oversimplifying or appropriating

modes.reason: Effective orientation requires three decisions: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what do they need to be told to follow what comes next. Making these decisions explicit before drafting prevents students from writing only for themselves.

nodes.label: Explaining and supporting decisions with data representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain decisions and conclusions related to an economic or business issue, supported by visual displays or data representations, and acknowledge research sources.
criteria: Supports at least one conclusion with a data representation (table, graph, or graphic organiser)
Explains what the representation shows and how it supports the conclusion
Acknowledges at least one research source

width.minimum: Write an explanation of one conclusion from an economic investigation, supported by one data representation (table, graph or graphic organiser), and acknowledge the source.
width.typical: Explain decisions and conclusions related to an economic or business issue supported by representations of relevant data — applying the elaboration examples (visual displays, graphic organisers, tables and graphs, explanations, procedures or reports). Acknowledge research findings formally. The explanation should: state the conclusion, show how the data representation supports it, explain the reasoning connecting data to conclusion, and cite the source.
wider: Construct a multi-representation explanation — using a combination of text, table, and graph to build an explanation that uses each representation for what it does best
Evaluate the data representations used in a published economic report and explain which are well-chosen for the conclusions they support and which are misleading or poorly matched

Apply formal acknowledgement conventions to a range of source types (government statistics, news articles, expert reports) and explain why proper acknowledgement matters for the credibility of economic arguments

modes.reason: Data-supported explanation requires repeated practice to build the habit of connecting the representation to the conclusion explicitly rather than inserting it as decoration. Students commonly include graphs without explaining what they show or why they support the claim.

nodes.label: Constructing reasoned arguments with appropriate tone
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present a reasoned argument in relation to an economic or business issue, applying tone appropriate to the purpose and audience.
criteria: States a clear position on the economic or business issue
Provides at least one evidence-based reason that supports the position
Applies a tone appropriate to the specified audience and purpose

width.minimum: Write one reasoned argument on an economic or business issue — stating a position, providing at least one evidence-based reason, and using a tone appropriate to a specified audience.
width.typical: Present a reasoned argument in relation to an economic or business issue applying tone appropriate to purpose — using the elaboration example (authoritative tone when explaining trends in data to peers or business representatives). The argument should: state a clear position on the issue; provide evidence-based reasons that support the position; address the issue's complexity; apply an authoritative, substantiated tone (not casual, not assertive without evidence); and acknowledge research findings. Distinguish an argument from an explanation — an argument stakes a position; an explanation describes how something works.
wider: Write arguments from competing stakeholder positions on the same economic issue (e.g. free trade vs protectionism from an industry perspective vs a consumer perspective) — demonstrating how evidence selection and framing differ by position
Evaluate two arguments on the same economic issue for reasoning quality — identifying which makes stronger use of evidence, more valid causal reasoning, and more appropriate tone
Write an argument that explicitly anticipates and addresses a counter-argument — explaining why acknowledging the counter-argument strengthens rather than weakens the overall argument

modes.reason: The argument structure (position → reason → evidence → explanation of how evidence supports reason) is new at Y9 and must be made explicit. Students commonly produce explanations that state conclusions without staking a position, or staking positions without evidence — neither is an argument.

Arguments in Economics and Business vary in tone and evidence demands across contexts (academic, business, policy, consumer). Practising across contexts — not just in one academic format — builds tone flexibility and evidence-selection judgment.

descriptors.title: Economic indicators
descriptors.description: how and why the economic indicators influence economic decision-making
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the role of Australia's financial sector and its effect on economic decision-making by individuals, businesses and global markets (AC9HE9K01). They understand how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government (AC9HE9K02). They can explain how economic decisions by one actor affect others across the system.

nodes.label: What economic indicators are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key economic indicators and describe what each measures about the economy.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish what different indicators measure will conflate them when explaining how each influences decision-making. Without this foundation, later nodes on government response become vague ('the government responds to bad numbers') rather than specific.
criteria: Names at least three distinct economic indicators and states what each measures
Distinguishes between indicators (e.g. can explain why unemployment and inflation measure different things)

width.minimum: Identify at least three economic indicators (e.g. GDP growth rate, unemployment rate, inflation rate) and state what each measures.
width.typical: Identify and explain a range of economic indicators including GDP growth, unemployment trends, inflation rates, and sustainability indexes; describe what each measures and what it signals about economic conditions.
wider: Investigate composite indexes such as the OECD Better Life Index or the Genuine Progress Indicator and evaluate what they add to traditional economic indicators
Compare how different countries select and weight economic indicators, examining how political context shapes measurement priorities
Explore leading, lagging and coincident indicators and explain how their timing affects how decision-makers use them

modes.reason: Introduce indicators systematically — what is being measured, what unit, over what period, and what direction signals concern. Students commonly conflate GDP and employment, or confuse inflation with interest rates. A structured note-taking scaffold per indicator prevents this.
Build a reference set of indicators that students can draw on throughout the unit. Class-constructed reference cards or a shared table work well here.

nodes.label: Interpreting indicator data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and interpret indicator data — identifying trends, describing what a change in direction signals, and using appropriate economic vocabulary.
nodes.hinge_reason: The rest of the descriptor requires students to explain how indicators *influence* decisions — this is only possible if they can read what the indicators are saying. Students who cannot interpret a trend cannot explain why a government might respond.
criteria: Correctly describes the trend shown in a provided indicator dataset (rising, falling, stable, volatile)
Uses at least one specific economic term accurately when describing what the trend signals

width.minimum: Read a provided graph or table for one indicator; describe the trend and state what a rise or fall signals.
width.typical: Interpret data for multiple indicators across a time period; describe trends, identify turning points, and use terms such as economic growth, recession, inflation, unemployment rate accurately.
wider: Analyse a period of economic volatility (e.g. GFC, COVID-19) using multiple indicator datasets to explain what happened and in what sequence
Compare Australian indicator trends with those of a trading partner to identify divergence and consider its implications
Evaluate the limitations of a specific indicator — what it misses, who it undercounts, or what it obscures

modes.reason: Practise reading graphs of different indicators with varied time periods. Common errors include misreading rate-of-change (confusing a slowing growth rate with a decline), or misinterpreting unemployment — knowing fluency here prevents errors in later analysis.
Expose students to data from different economic events and time periods so they can apply interpretation skills across varied contexts rather than pattern-matching to a single example.

nodes.label: Government economic objectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and explain the Australian Government's key economic objectives and connect each to one or more indicators that track progress toward it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding that indicators are proxies for objectives — that GDP is tracked because growth is a goal — students cannot explain *why* indicators matter to decision-making. They will describe reaction without understanding rationale.
criteria: Names at least two government economic objectives and explains why each matters for Australians
Correctly matches each objective to the indicator(s) used to track it

width.minimum: Name at least two government economic objectives (e.g. economic growth, full employment, price stability) and identify which indicator tracks each.
width.typical: Explain the Australian Government's main economic objectives — economic growth, full employment and price stability — and explain why each matters for living standards; connect each objective to its corresponding indicator(s).
wider: Investigate how environmental sustainability or wellbeing has been framed as a policy objective and which indicators governments are beginning to use to track it
Compare Australia's stated economic objectives with those of a different country and examine whether the same indicators are used
Examine how objectives can conflict (e.g. low unemployment can drive inflation) and how governments balance competing indicators

modes.reason: Help students build the explicit connection: objective → what it means → why it matters → which indicator tracks it → what direction signals concern. This logic chain is the scaffold for the integration node.

nodes.label: How indicators prompt government response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how changes in specific indicators trigger or justify government economic decisions, using examples of actual or hypothetical government responses.
criteria: Explains a government decision with reference to a specific indicator change that preceded it
Names the economic objective the response was intended to serve

width.minimum: Describe one example of a government response to a change in an economic indicator, explaining the connection between the indicator movement and the decision.
width.typical: Explain how the Australian Government may intervene in response to emerging economic issues or changes in indicators — such as responding to declining GDP with fiscal stimulus, or to rising inflation with interest rate signals — with reference to economic objectives.
wider: Analyse a specific historical case of government intervention (e.g. fiscal stimulus during GFC, COVID-19 JobKeeper) and evaluate whether the indicator signal justified the response
Investigate how international organisations (IMF, World Bank) use economic indicators to issue recommendations to governments and assess whether governments follow them
Examine the role of the Reserve Bank of Australia in interpreting inflation data and adjusting the cash rate, tracing the decision chain from indicator to policy

modes.reason: Use multiple real-world examples of government response across different indicator triggers so students can generalise the mechanism rather than memorise one case.

nodes.label: Indicators and individual/business decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how economic indicators influence decision-making beyond government — by businesses and individuals — and describe the logic of these responses.
criteria: Gives a specific example of how an indicator influences a decision by a non-government actor (business or individual)
Explains the reasoning behind the decision — why this indicator matters to this actor

width.minimum: Give one example of how an economic indicator (e.g. rising unemployment or inflation) affects a decision made by a business or individual consumer.
width.typical: Explain how indicators such as employment statistics, inflation rates and GDP growth influence decision-making by businesses (e.g. investment, hiring, pricing) and individuals (e.g. spending, saving, borrowing), and connect these to the broader economic picture.
wider: Investigate how consumer confidence surveys (a leading indicator) influence business investment decisions and explain the transmission mechanism
Analyse how a small business owner in a specific sector would interpret a suite of current indicators to make a decision about expansion or staffing
Compare how high-income and low-income households respond differently to the same indicator signal (e.g. rising interest rates) and examine equity implications

modes.reason: This node brings together indicator knowledge, government objectives and real-world actors into the full scope of the descriptor — how and why indicators influence economic decision-making across all actors. It synthesises the prior nodes.

descriptors.title: Government economic intervention
descriptors.description: the ways that government intervenes in the economy to improve economic performance and living standards within Australian society
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government (AC9HE9K02). They have explored how Australia trades with other nations and its patterns with Asia (AC9HE9K03). They can explain how different actors in the economy interact and how decisions ripple across the system. Students have also begun working with AC9HE10K01 — how economic indicators signal the need for government response.

nodes.label: What government intervention means
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why markets alone do not always produce desirable outcomes and why governments intervene in the economy.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that intervention is a response to a problem — not an arbitrary action — will describe policies without explaining their purpose. The rationale is the connective tissue linking indicator signals (K01) to specific policy tools.
criteria: States at least two reasons why governments intervene in the economy
Connects a reason for intervention to a category of government tool (e.g. inequality → redistribution)

width.minimum: State at least two reasons why the Australian Government intervenes in the economy (e.g. to address market failure, improve living standards, reduce inequality).
width.typical: Explain the rationale for government intervention — market failure, inequality, unemployment and poverty — and identify the general categories of government tools available (fiscal policy, income redistribution, regulation).
wider: Examine a specific market failure (e.g. pollution, public goods provision, monopoly) and evaluate why the market alone cannot address it
Compare the case for and against government intervention using a contemporary Australian policy debate (e.g. housing affordability, energy markets)
Investigate how views on the appropriate scope of government intervention have changed over time in Australia

modes.reason: Build the logic chain: what the market produces without intervention → what problem this creates → what the government can do about it. This scaffold prevents students from treating policies as a list to memorise rather than responses to economic conditions.

nodes.label: Fiscal policy and the federal Budget
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the Australian Government uses fiscal policy — taxation and expenditure — to influence economic performance and living standards.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fiscal policy is the primary instrument the descriptor names. Students who cannot explain the taxation-expenditure mechanism cannot meet the descriptor's scope — all downstream analysis of income redistribution and welfare depends on understanding how the Budget works.
criteria: Explains what fiscal policy is and distinguishes taxation from expenditure as tools
Gives a specific example of how a Budget measure is intended to influence an economic outcome

width.minimum: Explain what fiscal policy is and give one example each of how the government uses taxation and expenditure to influence the economy.
width.typical: Explain how the Australian Government uses fiscal policy to improve standard of living — including the federal Budget, taxation settings and expenditure on skills training and workforce development; distinguish between expansionary and contractionary fiscal stances.
wider: Analyse a specific federal Budget measure (e.g. infrastructure investment, skills package) and evaluate its expected impact on economic performance and who benefits
Compare the fiscal policy responses of Australia and another country to a shared economic shock and explain differences in approach
Investigate how automatic stabilisers (e.g. unemployment benefits) function as fiscal policy without requiring Budget decisions

modes.reason: Use multiple real Budget examples — infrastructure, social services, tax cuts — so students can apply the fiscal policy concept across varied contexts rather than memorising one example.

nodes.label: Income redistribution and living standards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how and why the government redistributes income, and identify the mechanisms through which redistribution affects living standards and inequality.
criteria: Distinguishes income transfers from universal service provision as redistribution mechanisms
Explains how at least one redistribution mechanism affects living standards for a specific group

width.minimum: Name one type of income transfer (e.g. pension, youth allowance) and one universal service (e.g. healthcare, education) and explain how each affects living standards.
width.typical: Explain how the government redistributes income to achieve a more equal distribution — including income transfers (pensions, youth allowance, job search) and provision of universal services (healthcare, education); explain the forces that create variation in living standards (unemployment, poverty) and why redistribution is a policy response.
wider: Investigate how Australia's Gini coefficient has changed over time and evaluate whether government redistribution has been effective in reducing inequality
Compare the scope and design of Australia's income support system with that of another country (e.g. Nordic model vs US model) and examine trade-offs
Examine how specific communities (e.g. First Nations Australians, regional communities) experience living standards variation and what targeted government responses exist

modes.reason: Variety of redistribution mechanisms prevents students from treating this as a single category. Differentiating income transfers from universal service provision clarifies the mechanism and enables more precise explanation.

nodes.label: The Reserve Bank and monetary policy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the role and function of the Reserve Bank of Australia and explain how monetary policy tools (particularly the cash rate) are used to manage economic performance.
criteria: States the RBA's primary mandate and one tool it uses
Explains how a change in the cash rate influences economic behaviour (even if the chain is simplified)

width.minimum: Identify the Reserve Bank of Australia's primary role and explain one way it influences the economy (e.g. through the cash rate).
width.typical: Explain the role and function of the RBA within the Australian economy — including its independence, inflation target mandate and use of the cash rate to influence borrowing costs, consumer spending and investment.
wider: Trace the transmission mechanism from RBA cash rate decision to household mortgage repayments to consumer spending to economic growth
Compare a period of rate rises (e.g. 2022–2023) with a period of rate cuts (e.g. 2020) and explain the RBA's stated reasoning in each case
Evaluate the limits of monetary policy — situations where interest rate adjustment does not produce expected economic outcomes

modes.reason: The transmission mechanism from RBA decision to economic outcomes involves multiple steps and can be confusing without explicit scaffolding. Map the chain clearly: RBA decision → bank interest rates → borrowing behaviour → spending → economic activity.

nodes.label: Government intervention — integrated evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain multiple ways the Australian Government intervenes in the economy and evaluate how these tools together aim to improve economic performance and living standards.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of government intervention and explains what each aims to achieve
Explains how both tools relate to improving economic performance or living standards

width.minimum: Explain two distinct ways the government intervenes (e.g. fiscal policy and income redistribution) and describe what each is trying to achieve.
width.typical: Explain how fiscal policy, income redistribution and monetary policy work together as a suite of government interventions aimed at improving economic performance and living standards; discuss variation in living standards and how government tools address it.
wider: Evaluate a current or recent government economic policy package, identifying which intervention types are present and assessing whether the mix is coherent
Investigate how the government's economic intervention approach has shifted under different political administrations and what this reveals about assumptions behind the tools
Examine how intervention affects different groups unequally — who benefits most from fiscal expansion, who bears the burden of monetary tightening

modes.reason: This node draws fiscal policy, redistribution and monetary policy together into a coherent picture of government economic management. The integration demand is the descriptor's full scope — explaining the *ways* (plural) of intervention.

descriptors.title: Major financial decisions
descriptors.description: factors that influence major consumer and financial decisions, and the short- and long-term consequences of these decisions
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how individuals and businesses manage consumer and financial risks and rewards (AC9HE9K05). They can identify financial risks, explain strategies for managing them, and consider trade-offs in financial decision-making. They have also explored how consumer decisions are influenced by market forces.

nodes.label: Minor vs major financial decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between minor and major consumer and financial decisions, and explain what makes a decision 'major' in terms of scale, commitment and consequence.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify what makes a decision major, the factors analysis in subsequent nodes becomes unanchored — they will apply the same analysis to any purchase rather than to the high-stakes decisions the descriptor targets.
criteria: Correctly classifies at least two decisions as minor and at least two as major with supporting reasons
Identifies at least one characteristic that distinguishes a major financial decision

width.minimum: Give examples of both minor and major consumer/financial decisions and explain at least one characteristic that makes a decision 'major' (e.g. size of commitment, difficulty to reverse, long-term impact).
width.typical: Identify and contrast examples of minor and major consumer and financial decisions; explain processes that guide decision-making and what distinguishes major decisions — scale of financial commitment, duration, difficulty of reversal, and significance of consequences.
wider: Investigate how a major decision (e.g. taking out a student loan) affects financial decision-making for years afterward — tracing opportunity costs and constrained choices
Compare how major financial decisions differ across life stages (school leaver, mid-career, pre-retirement) and explain why the same decision may be major at one stage and minor at another
Examine how cognitive biases (e.g. present bias, overconfidence) affect how people categorise decisions as major or minor and what this means for decision quality

modes.reason: Build a clear set of criteria that define a major financial decision. Concrete examples (buying a car, taking a personal loan, choosing a mobile plan on contract) anchor the abstract criteria.

nodes.label: Factors influencing major decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse multiple factors that influence major consumer and financial decisions, including economic, personal and ethical factors.
nodes.hinge_reason: This node contains the descriptor's primary analytical demand. Students who cannot identify and explain the full factor range will produce surface-level analysis in assessments and cannot connect factors to consequences in the next node.
criteria: Identifies at least three distinct factors and explains how each influences a named major financial decision
Explains how at least two factors interact or reinforce each other in the same decision

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least three factors that influence a major financial decision (e.g. price, availability of finance, marketing, age of consumer).
width.typical: Analyse the range of factors that influence major consumer and financial decisions: price, availability and cost of finance, marketing of products, age and gender of consumer, convenience, and ethical and environmental considerations; explain how different factors interact in a real decision scenario.
wider: Investigate how targeted digital marketing (e.g. social media algorithms, buy-now-pay-later integration) shapes consumer financial decisions, especially for young people
Compare how ethical and environmental considerations influence financial decisions differently across demographic groups and examine what drives these differences
Analyse a major financial product (e.g. a car loan, a home loan) by working through all the listed factors and explaining how each shapes the decision landscape

modes.reason: Build a reference set of factors through varied examples — not just one case. Students need to see that different factors dominate in different decision contexts.

Marketing, finance availability and ethical considerations are richer as width directions — applying the factor framework to different decision types (housing, vehicle, education) reveals which factors are constant and which are context-specific.

nodes.label: Short- and long-term consequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain both the short- and long-term consequences of major financial decisions, distinguishing costs from benefits across different time horizons.
criteria: Distinguishes at least one short-term and one long-term consequence for a named major financial decision
Correctly identifies whether each consequence is a cost or a benefit and provides supporting reasoning

width.minimum: For one major financial decision, identify at least one short-term and one long-term consequence, distinguishing whether each is a cost or a benefit.
width.typical: Analyse the short- and long-term costs and benefits of major consumer and financial decisions — including ability to make loan repayments, available savings, depreciation, maintenance costs and insurance, as well as benefits such as independence and convenience (e.g. for purchasing a car or home).
wider: Model the total cost of ownership of a specific major purchase (e.g. a car) over 5 years, accounting for depreciation, insurance, fuel, maintenance and opportunity cost of capital
Compare two financing pathways for the same major purchase (e.g. cash vs loan vs lease) and evaluate which produces better long-term outcomes under different assumptions
Investigate how a major financial decision taken early in life (e.g. student debt, early home purchase) constrains or enables subsequent financial decisions through compound effects

modes.reason: Vary the major decision context — vehicle purchase, home purchase, personal loan — so students can identify which consequences are universal (opportunity cost, ongoing repayment commitment) and which are specific to the decision type.

nodes.label: Factors and consequences — integrated analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse factors influencing a major financial decision and connect these to predicted short- and long-term consequences, demonstrating integrated understanding of the descriptor.
criteria: Analyses a named major financial decision by identifying at least two factors and at least one consequence per factor
Distinguishes between short- and long-term consequences and explains at least one trade-off in the decision

width.minimum: For one major financial decision, explain two influencing factors and one consequence that flows from each factor.
width.typical: Analyse a major financial decision by identifying the key influencing factors, explaining how they shape the decision, and evaluating the likely short- and long-term consequences — including trade-offs between convenience, cost and long-term financial wellbeing.
wider: Analyse a real case study (e.g. a young person taking on a car loan with high interest while receiving youth allowance) using the full factor and consequence framework
Evaluate how the ability to 'opt out' if circumstances change should be factored into a major financial decision, and apply this to a real product comparison
Design a decision-making guide for a specific major financial decision targeted at a Year 10 audience, demonstrating command of factors and consequences

modes.reason: The integration demand is the descriptor's full scope — analysing factors *and* consequences together. This node is where students demonstrate that they can connect the analytical moves from nodes 2 and 3 into a coherent account of a specific decision.

descriptors.title: Superannuation system
