descriptors.description: the importance of Australia's superannuation system and how this system affects consumer and financial decision-making
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand factors that influence major consumer and financial decisions and their short- and long-term consequences (AC9HE10K03). They can analyse how financial commitments accumulate over time and consider the role of savings. Students have also explored how governments redistribute income through transfers and services (AC9HE10K02).

nodes.label: What superannuation is and why it exists
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what superannuation is, why Australia introduced a compulsory super system, and the dual purpose it serves for individuals and government.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who see superannuation only as savings for retirement — without understanding the government's fiscal rationale — cannot explain the system's design features (compulsion, tax treatment, preservation rules). The dual rationale is foundational.
criteria: Explains what superannuation is in terms of how it works (regular contributions, investment, access at retirement)
States both the individual wellbeing and government fiscal rationale for compulsory super

width.minimum: Explain what superannuation is and state at least two reasons why Australia has a compulsory superannuation system.
width.typical: Explain the importance of Australia's superannuation system in relation to human and financial wellbeing in retirement, and explain why the system also serves the government's ability to maintain a welfare payment system — reducing future pension dependency.
wider: Investigate how Australia's superannuation system compares internationally — examining countries with defined benefit vs accumulation models and what trade-offs each involves
Analyse the history of superannuation in Australia — why it was introduced in the 1990s, at what rate, and how it has evolved to today's rate
Examine how the ageing population creates pressure on government welfare payments and evaluate how superannuation is intended to reduce this pressure

modes.reason: Build both rationales explicitly: individual retirement income security AND reduced government pension liability. Students commonly grasp the individual rationale but miss the systemic one. The systemic rationale explains compulsion and tax incentives.

nodes.label: How a super fund works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how an individual superannuation fund operates — who contributes, how it is taxed, and how the fund grows over time.
criteria: Identifies employer and employee as contributors and describes the employer's compulsory obligation
Explains at least one tax feature of superannuation (e.g. concessional tax on contributions or earnings)

width.minimum: Identify who contributes to a superannuation fund and explain at least one tax feature of the system.
width.typical: Explain how individuals manage a personal superannuation fund: who contributes (employer, employee, government co-contribution), how contributions are taxed, how to consolidate funds, how to find lost super, and how to track account performance.
wider: Model the compound growth of a superannuation account over a working life, varying contribution rates and investment options to show the effect of early vs late contributions
Investigate the implications of employment gaps (e.g. career breaks, casual work, unpaid care) on superannuation balance at retirement and who is most affected
Examine the gender superannuation gap — why women retire with significantly less super than men — and evaluate policy responses

modes.reason: Vary the worked examples — different employment types, contribution levels, and life stages — so students understand that super outcomes vary significantly depending on individual circumstances.

nodes.label: Super investment decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why individuals make decisions about superannuation investment options and how personal circumstances affect these decisions.
criteria: Names at least two personal circumstance factors that influence investment option choice
Explains the general relationship between investment risk and return, and how this relates to time horizon

width.minimum: State at least two factors related to personal circumstances that might influence which super investment option a person chooses (e.g. age, employment status).
width.typical: Explain why individuals choose different superannuation investment options (growth, balanced, conservative, ethical) based on circumstances including age, employment status, number of dependants, and anticipated retirement age; explain the relationship between investment risk and likely return over time.
wider: Investigate the growth of ethical and ESG (environmental, social, governance) superannuation options and evaluate whether ethical investing compromises returns
Analyse how investment option selection changes across a working life — why a 25-year-old and a 60-year-old should typically choose differently — using the concept of investment horizon
Compare how self-managed super funds (SMSFs) differ from industry and retail funds and evaluate the circumstances in which an SMSF might be appropriate

modes.reason: Different personal profiles (young casual worker, mid-career professional, near-retirement worker) illustrate how the same system produces different optimal strategies. Vary the scenario rather than deepening analysis of one profile.

nodes.label: Superannuation and broader financial decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the existence of superannuation affects other consumer and financial decisions — including career choices, savings behaviour, insurance, and planning for retirement.
criteria: Identifies at least one way that superannuation influences a financial decision outside of super itself
Explains how employment type (e.g. casual, part-time, permanent) affects superannuation outcomes

width.minimum: Give one example of how superannuation affects a non-super financial decision (e.g. how super balance affects decisions about additional voluntary contributions or salary sacrifice).
width.typical: Explain how superannuation shapes broader consumer and financial decision-making — including how people think about retirement income, whether to salary sacrifice, how to balance super with other savings goals, and how employment decisions (e.g. casual vs permanent work) affect super outcomes.
wider: Investigate the interaction between superannuation and the Age Pension means test — how super balance affects eligibility and what this implies for optimal drawdown strategy
Evaluate the financial implications of taking paid vs unpaid parental leave on super and lifetime retirement savings
Examine how superannuation death benefits and estate planning interact, and why beneficiary nominations matter

modes.reason: This node integrates the system design, operational mechanics, and investment choices into the broader picture of how super shapes financial decision-making across a working life. It completes the descriptor's second demand — how super affects consumer and financial decision-making.

descriptors.title: Workforce productivity
descriptors.description: processes that businesses use to manage the workforce and improve productivity, including the role of entrepreneurs
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand processes businesses use to create and maintain competitive advantage, including the role of entrepreneurs (AC9HE9K04). They can explain how businesses respond to market conditions, manage risk and use innovation to maintain advantage. They have a working understanding of business structures and strategy at Year 9 level.

nodes.label: Workforce management processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain strategies businesses use to manage their workforce effectively, including organisational structures, decision-making culture and employee conditions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Workforce management is the first of two distinct areas in this descriptor. Students who cannot distinguish between management strategies (structure, culture, conditions) and productivity strategies (training, technology, R&D) will conflate the two in assessments.
criteria: Names at least two distinct workforce management strategies and explains the purpose of each
Explains how at least one strategy improves workforce engagement or performance

width.minimum: Identify at least two workforce management strategies (e.g. organisational structure choices, flexible work arrangements) and explain how each can improve workforce performance.
width.typical: Identify and explain strategies for improving workforce management — horizontal vs vertical organisational structures, transparency in decision-making, encouraging initiative, paid parental leave, flexible work arrangements, employer responsibilities to workers and government; explain how each strategy affects workforce engagement and performance.
wider: Investigate how workplace flexibility (e.g. remote work, compressed weeks) affects productivity outcomes and evaluate the evidence for and against flexible work arrangements
Compare horizontal and vertical organisational structures in a real industry context and evaluate which structure suits different business types and scales

Examine First Nations Australian workforce participation initiatives (e.g. cross-cultural training, 'Closing the Gap' commitments, corporate diversity commitments) and evaluate their design and impact

modes.reason: Distinguish workforce *management* (how the business organises, motivates and supports its people) from productivity *improvement* (how the business enables people to produce more). Students frequently run these together.

Apply workforce management strategies to varied business types — small business, corporation, government organisation — so students can see which strategies are universal and which depend on scale or sector.

nodes.label: Productivity improvement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain strategies that businesses use to improve productivity, including training, capital investment, R&D and technology applications.
criteria: Names at least two productivity improvement strategies with different mechanisms (e.g. one human capital, one technology)
Explains how a named strategy is expected to increase output, reduce costs or improve quality

width.minimum: Identify at least two strategies for improving productivity and explain how each is expected to increase output or reduce input.
width.typical: Identify and explain productivity improvement strategies — training and upskilling, capital investment, increasing R&D, investment in technology applications, use of just-in-time inventory systems, and collection and analysis of data to inform product development or service delivery; explain the mechanism by which each improves productivity.
wider: Investigate how a specific technology application (e.g. automation, AI-assisted logistics, data analytics) has changed productivity in a named industry and evaluate costs and benefits of adoption
Examine the productivity paradox — why significant technology investment has not always produced proportionate productivity gains — and evaluate explanations
Compare just-in-time inventory against traditional buffer-stock approaches and evaluate the productivity and risk trade-offs of each

modes.reason: Apply productivity strategies to varied industry contexts — manufacturing, services, healthcare — so students understand which strategies generalise and which are sector-specific.

nodes.label: The role of entrepreneurs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how entrepreneurs lead responses to economic and technological change, including in the context of Australian First Nations businesses and support organisations.
criteria: Explains what distinguishes entrepreneurial activity from standard business management
Gives a specific example of an entrepreneur responding to an economic or technological change

width.minimum: Explain what an entrepreneur does and give one example of how entrepreneurial activity responds to economic change.
width.typical: Explain how entrepreneurs lead responses to changes in global and domestic economic conditions and use technologies to drive innovation — for example, influencing approaches to waste management or sustainable energy; investigate support structures for start-up businesses including those for First Nations Australian entrepreneurs.
wider: Investigate a specific Australian entrepreneur whose work responds to an economic or environmental challenge and evaluate the impact of their innovation

Examine First Nations Australian businesses supported by organisations such as the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations or First Nations Chambers of Commerce and evaluate how these structures enable entrepreneurship
Compare the support ecosystems for entrepreneurs across different countries and evaluate which features of the Australian system are distinctive or effective

modes.reason: Build a range of entrepreneurial examples across industries and contexts — including First Nations entrepreneurs — so students have a diverse reference set rather than a single prototype case.

nodes.label: Workforce management and productivity — integrated
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how workforce management and productivity improvement strategies work together, and how entrepreneurial leadership connects to both, to drive business performance.
criteria: Explains a connection between workforce management and a productivity outcome
Identifies the role of entrepreneurial leadership in at least one of the two areas (management culture or innovation)

width.minimum: Explain one connection between a workforce management strategy and a productivity outcome — how managing people well creates conditions for improved productivity.
width.typical: Explain how workforce management (structure, culture, conditions) creates the organisational context in which productivity strategies (training, technology, data use) can succeed; explain the role of entrepreneurial leadership in driving both workforce culture and innovation.
wider: Analyse a real business case where workforce management and productivity improvement were integrated as a deliberate strategy and evaluate outcomes

Evaluate how a First Nations business or enterprise (e.g. an Indigenous corporation, social enterprise) manages workforce and productivity in ways that reflect cultural values alongside commercial goals

Investigate how high-productivity organisations differ from low-productivity ones in the same industry, identifying whether workforce management or technology investment is the more important differentiating factor

modes.reason: This node brings the descriptor's three components — workforce management, productivity strategies, entrepreneurship — into a coherent account of how businesses manage the workforce and improve productivity. It completes the descriptor's full scope.

descriptors.title: Develop and modify inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop and modify questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop and modify questions to investigate a contemporary economic and business issue at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S01). They have practised formulating inquiry questions and hypotheses in economic contexts, and have some experience modifying questions to narrow or focus an investigation. The Y10 descriptor carries the same wording — the progression is in the complexity of issues investigated and the sophistication of question modification.

nodes.label: Features of good economic inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what makes an economic inquiry question investigable — specific, empirically grounded, and connected to a real contemporary issue.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish an investigable question from a vague or rhetorical one will produce unfocused investigations. Modification in node 2 only works if students can diagnose what is wrong with a question first.
criteria: Identifies at least two features of a well-formed economic inquiry question
Correctly selects the stronger question from a pair and provides at least one valid reason

width.minimum: Given two or three example questions of varying quality, identify which is most investigable and explain at least one reason why.
width.typical: Explain the features of a well-formed economic inquiry question — specificity, empirical groundedness, contemporary relevance, and scope that is neither too broad nor too narrow; distinguish investigable questions from rhetorical or opinion questions.
wider: Compare a research hypothesis (e.g. 'Responding to an upswing in the economy with expansionary measures will improve business productivity') with an inquiry question and explain when each is more appropriate
Analyse the questions posed in real economic reports or policy documents and evaluate how well they focus the investigation
Design a rubric for evaluating the quality of an economic inquiry question and apply it to a set of examples

modes.reason: Use worked examples of weak vs strong questions with explicit annotation of what makes each stronger. Criteria need to be explicit before students can apply them independently.

nodes.label: Developing and modifying questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop an initial inquiry question about a contemporary economic or business issue and modify it to improve its investigability — narrowing scope, increasing specificity, or reframing to enable empirical investigation.
criteria: Produces at least one modification to a draft inquiry question and articulates what it improves
The modified question is demonstrably more specific or investigable than the original

width.minimum: Draft one inquiry question about a contemporary economic issue and make at least one modification that improves its focus, explaining what the modification achieves.
width.typical: Develop a range of questions to investigate a complex issue; modify questions to improve focus — for example, moving from broad questions like 'What factors influence decision-making in consumer and financial contexts?' to specific ones like 'What factors influence choosing a mobile phone plan?'; explain what each modification achieves and why it improves the investigation.
wider: Develop both an inquiry question and a related hypothesis for the same economic issue and explain the different investigative strategies each requires
Take a real economic question from a government report or media source and modify it to make it more investigable for a school-based inquiry
Investigate how economists frame research questions differently from journalists reporting on the same issue, and evaluate what each framing enables or constrains

modes.reason: Practise the modification move across multiple questions and multiple economic topics. Students need repeated cycles of draft-modify-explain to build fluency in this capability.

descriptors.title: Locate, select and analyse information
descriptors.description: locate, select and analyse information and data from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate, select and analyse information and data from a range of sources at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S02). They have practised searching for economic information, evaluating sources for relevance and reliability, and using digital tools to organise data. Y10 builds on this with more complex sources, more contextually specific search strategies, and explicit attention to assumptions and missing information in sources.

nodes.label: Locating sources using contextually specific search
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use contextually specific search strategies to locate relevant economic and business sources, including using appropriate terminology and criteria.
criteria: Uses at least two contextually specific search terms derived from the inquiry question
Locates at least two sources that are relevant to the inquiry question

width.minimum: Use at least two contextually specific search terms or criteria (e.g. 'global markets', 'trade agreements Australia case studies') to locate sources relevant to an inquiry question.
width.typical: Locate online sources using contextually specific terms (e.g. 'global markets', 'fiscal policy Australia 2024') and criteria (e.g. key words to find 'case studies related to trade agreements'); explain how search strategy affects the quality and relevance of sources found.
wider: Compare the results of searching the same topic using a general search engine vs an academic database or government statistical portal and evaluate the difference in source quality
Develop a search protocol for a complex economic inquiry — including Boolean operators, date filters and domain restrictions — and evaluate what the protocol is designed to achieve
Investigate how algorithmic filtering in online search affects what economic information people find and evaluate implications for informed decision-making

modes.reason: Practise the search strategy move across multiple economic topics. Students need to internalise the connection between inquiry question → relevant search terms → source quality before they can reliably find usable sources.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for relevance and reliability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate economic information and data sources for relevance and reliability, using explicit criteria including who collected the data, when, and for what purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: The reliability evaluation move is what the descriptor's 'analyse' demand requires. Students who accept sources uncritically cannot complete the inquiry work the descriptor specifies — their findings will be built on unstated assumptions or unreliable data.
criteria: Applies at least two named criteria to evaluate a source's relevance or reliability
Identifies at least one assumption or missing information in a source that could affect its reliability

width.minimum: Apply at least two relevance or reliability criteria to evaluate a provided economic source.
width.typical: Select and analyse economic information and data for relevance (asking: How will this help answer the inquiry question?) and reliability (asking: How and when was the data collected? Who collected it? For what purpose?); explain assumptions or missing information that may affect reliability.
wider: Compare two sources presenting conflicting economic data on the same issue (e.g. different unemployment measures) and evaluate which is more reliable for a specific inquiry purpose
Investigate how government statistical agencies (ABS) and advocacy groups may present different data on the same economic phenomenon and explain how purpose shapes data collection and presentation
Evaluate a secondary source (news article, commentary) against its primary data source and identify what has been changed, emphasised or omitted in the reporting

modes.reason: Make the evaluation criteria explicit and practise applying them to real economic sources. Students commonly evaluate 'quality' vaguely — the structured criteria (who, when, purpose, assumptions) need to become habitual.

Apply reliability evaluation to different source types — ABS data, Reserve Bank reports, media articles, advocacy group reports — so students develop differentiated criteria rather than applying the same checklist uniformly.

nodes.label: Representing and using information with digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and represent economic information using specialised digital tools to support interpretation and analysis of an inquiry.
criteria: Represents economic information in an organised format that is connected to the inquiry question
Explains how the representation supports analysis (what it makes visible or easier to compare)

width.minimum: Represent economic information in at least one organised format (e.g. table, graphic organiser, annotated chart) that supports interpretation of the inquiry question.
width.typical: Select and represent information and data about an economic or business issue using specialised digital tools and processes to support interpretation and analysis — for example, a graphic organiser connecting government economic objectives with examples of intervention; an annotated data table showing trends.
wider: Use data visualisation tools (e.g. Canva, Datawrapper, spreadsheet charting) to represent and interpret economic trend data, explaining what the representation reveals that raw data does not
Design a multi-source synthesis document that represents economic information from three or more sources in a way that enables comparison and analysis
Evaluate the representational choices in an existing economic infographic or data dashboard and assess what those choices emphasise or obscure

modes.reason: Apply digital representation to varied data types — trend data, comparative data, causal relationship data — so students develop flexible tool use rather than competence with only one format.

descriptors.title: Interpret and predict economic impacts
descriptors.description: interpret information and data, explaining economic and business issues, trends and economic cause-and-effect relationships, and make predictions about consumer and financial impacts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret information and data, explain economic and business issues, trends and cause-and-effect relationships, and make predictions at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S03). They have practised interpreting single-variable economic data, identifying trends and articulating cause-and-effect logic. Y10 builds on this with multi-variable data, more complex trend interpretation and more explicit prediction reasoning.

nodes.label: Explaining economic issues from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret information to explain the nature, extent and importance of an economic or business issue.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot move from data to explanation — from 'this is what the data shows' to 'this is what it means about the issue' — they cannot produce the analytical outputs the descriptor requires. Trend identification without interpretation is a persistent failure mode.
criteria: States what a piece of data shows about an economic issue (description)
Explains what this means about the nature or extent of the issue (interpretation beyond description)

width.minimum: Interpret a provided data source about an economic issue and explain in at least two sentences what the data shows about the nature or extent of the issue.
width.typical: Interpret information to explain the nature, extent and importance of an economic or business issue — for example, the relationship between standards of living, infant mortality and access to health services; explain what the data reveals and why the issue matters.
wider: Interpret data about a complex multi-dimensional issue (e.g. housing affordability involving income, interest rates, housing supply and geographic distribution) and explain the interaction between factors
Evaluate how different data sources on the same issue can support different interpretations, and explain what this means for evidence-based decision-making
Investigate a global economic issue (e.g. supply chain disruption, climate-related economic risk) using international data and explain its implications for Australia

modes.reason: Make the explanation move explicit: what does this data show → what does this mean about the issue → why does this matter? Students who stay at description need scaffolding to take the interpretive step.

nodes.label: Interpreting multi-variable trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret multi-variable data to analyse trends over time, explaining reasons for changes and what the trend reveals about economic conditions.
criteria: Correctly identifies the trend shown in a multi-variable dataset
Provides at least one plausible reason for a change in direction in the trend, supported by the data

width.minimum: Interpret a provided multi-variable dataset (e.g. two indicators over time) and identify the trend and at least one reason for a change in direction.
width.typical: Interpret multi-variable data to analyse trends in economic activity over time — for example, trends in government health and education expenditure; explain reasons for changes in the trend and what the pattern reveals about priorities or conditions.
wider: Analyse an economic trend using three or more variables to identify leading and lagging relationships (e.g. how business investment precedes employment growth by 6–12 months)
Compare trends across two countries for the same economic variable and explain divergence or convergence over a significant period
Evaluate how a trend visualisation (e.g. a time series chart) can be presented to emphasise different interpretations, and what this means for data literacy

modes.reason: Practise multi-variable trend interpretation across different economic domains — government spending, employment, trade, household income. Fluency requires repeated application.

nodes.label: Cause-and-effect analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse causes and effects of an economic issue — explaining why the issue arises and what its consequences are for individuals, businesses or the broader economy.
nodes.hinge_reason: Cause-and-effect reasoning is the core analytical demand of this descriptor. Students who can describe trends but cannot explain why they happen — or what happens as a result — cannot produce the causal analysis the descriptor requires.
criteria: States a cause-and-effect relationship for an economic issue with at least one intermediate mechanism explained
Identifies at least one group affected by the effect and explains why they are affected

width.minimum: For one economic issue, state at least one cause and one effect, explaining the connection between them.
width.typical: Analyse the causes and effects of an economic issue on individuals or businesses — for example, the reasons for and implications of government intervention in the economy to improve living standards; explain the chain of causation and identify who is affected and how.
wider: Map a multi-step causal chain (e.g. rising inflation → RBA cash rate increase → higher mortgage repayments → reduced consumer spending → slower growth) and evaluate where the chain might break
Analyse how the same economic cause produces different effects on different groups (e.g. rising interest rates affect renters, mortgage-holders and savers differently)
Investigate an economic issue where the cause-and-effect relationship is contested and evaluate competing explanations using evidence

modes.reason: Build causal chains explicitly: cause → mechanism → effect. The mechanism step is where students most often default to assertion. Modelling multi-step chains with identifiable mechanisms is the key scaffold.
Apply causal analysis to varied economic issues — government intervention, consumer decisions, trade — so students generalise the analytical move rather than memorising one causal chain.

nodes.label: Making predictions about consumer and financial impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse trends and cause-and-effect relationships to make reasoned predictions about who will be affected and how, with reference to economic evidence.
criteria: Makes a specific prediction about consumer or financial impacts connected to a named trend or causal relationship
Provides explicit reasoning for the prediction — the mechanism that links the trend to the predicted outcome

width.minimum: Based on a provided trend or causal analysis, make one prediction about consumer or financial impacts and explain the reasoning behind it.
width.typical: Analyse trends to make predictions about who will be affected and how — for example, trends in productivity and implications for businesses; explain the reasoning underpinning the prediction and acknowledge conditions under which it might not hold.
wider: Make a conditional prediction — 'if [economic condition], then [consumer/financial impact], because [mechanism]' — and evaluate the quality of the prediction against evidence of what actually happened
Compare predictions made by different economic commentators about the same trend and evaluate whose reasoning was most sound in retrospect
Investigate how businesses use economic trend data to make investment and staffing predictions and evaluate how prediction quality affects business outcomes

modes.reason: Prediction integrates interpretation, trend analysis and causal reasoning into a single forward-looking claim. This is the descriptor's full demand — the ability to use economic evidence to reason about likely future impacts.

descriptors.title: Evaluate and decide using cost-benefit
descriptors.description: develop and evaluate a response to an economic and business issue, using cost-benefit analysis or criteria to decide on a course of action
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop and evaluate responses to economic and business issues using cost-benefit analysis or criteria at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S04). They have practised identifying and weighing costs and benefits to justify a decision, and have used criteria-based evaluation in business contexts. Y10 builds on this with more complex financial calculations, multi-variable cost-benefit analysis, and the explicit use of opportunity cost reasoning.

nodes.label: What cost-benefit analysis involves
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what cost-benefit analysis involves and identify the types of costs and benefits relevant to economic and business decisions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat cost-benefit analysis as a simple list of pros and cons — without understanding that costs and benefits must be identified systematically, valued and compared — cannot produce the structured evaluation the descriptor requires.
criteria: Explains what cost-benefit analysis is and how it differs from a simple list of pros and cons
Identifies at least two types of costs and two types of benefits relevant to a named decision

width.minimum: Explain what cost-benefit analysis is and identify at least two types of costs and two types of benefits that might be considered in a financial decision.
width.typical: Explain cost-benefit analysis as a structured approach to comparing the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of a course of action; identify types of costs (financial, opportunity, social, environmental) and benefits (financial returns, non-financial gains, social value) relevant to economic and business decisions.
wider: Investigate how governments use formal cost-benefit analysis in infrastructure or policy decisions and evaluate the challenges of assigning monetary values to non-financial costs and benefits
Compare cost-benefit analysis with criteria-based evaluation (e.g. using efficiency, profitability or equity as criteria) and explain when each approach is more appropriate
Examine how the same decision can produce very different cost-benefit outcomes depending on who bears the costs and who receives the benefits

modes.reason: Make the structure of CBA explicit: identify all relevant costs and benefits → assign relative weight or value → compare → conclude. The systematic nature of the method is what distinguishes it from informal pros-and-cons thinking.

nodes.label: Opportunity cost
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the opportunity cost in a decision and explain how it affects the evaluation of a course of action.
nodes.hinge_reason: Opportunity cost is the distinct economic reasoning tool in this descriptor. Without it, student evaluation reduces to identifying immediate financial costs and misses the comparative logic that defines economic decision analysis.
criteria: Correctly defines opportunity cost in own words
Identifies the opportunity cost in a named decision and explains how it should factor into the evaluation

width.minimum: Define opportunity cost and give one example of an opportunity cost in a consumer or business decision.
width.typical: Explain opportunity cost as the value of the next-best alternative foregone; apply opportunity cost reasoning to consumer and business decisions — for example, employing more staff instead of upskilling existing staff to improve productivity — and explain how opportunity cost affects the evaluation of a choice.
wider: Apply opportunity cost reasoning to a government policy decision (e.g. investing in public transport vs road infrastructure) and evaluate whether the opportunity cost is acknowledged in public debate
Investigate how sunk cost fallacy can distort decision-making by causing people to ignore opportunity costs in favour of costs already committed
Compare how a business and an individual household would calculate the opportunity cost of the same decision differently, and explain why

modes.reason: Opportunity cost reasoning needs to become automatic — practise applying it to multiple contexts (consumer, business, government) until students routinely ask 'what is being given up?' rather than only 'what does this cost?'.

nodes.label: Evaluating short- and long-term financial implications
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the short- and long-term financial implications of a decision, including calculating costs across time and considering flexibility to exit.
criteria: Identifies at least one short-term and one long-term financial implication for a named decision
Explains how the time horizon changes the relative weight given to costs or benefits

width.minimum: For one financial decision, identify at least one short-term and one long-term financial implication and explain how the time horizon affects the evaluation.
width.typical: Evaluate the short- and long-term financial implications of a decision — including calculating the costs of different purchasing methods, considering ability to opt out if circumstances change, and comparing loans or financing options to estimate total cost over time.
wider: Compare two financing pathways for a major consumer purchase (e.g. personal loan vs buy-now-pay-later vs savings) calculating total cost including interest, fees and opportunity cost for each
Evaluate how the ability to exit or reverse a decision (e.g. lease vs buy, variable vs fixed rate loan) should factor into a cost-benefit analysis
Investigate how businesses evaluate capital investment decisions over multi-year time horizons, including concepts of payback period and return on investment

modes.reason: Apply short/long-term financial analysis to varied decision contexts — consumer purchases, business investment, government spending — so students can apply time-horizon reasoning flexibly.

nodes.label: Evaluating using criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a response to an economic issue using explicit criteria (e.g. efficiency, profitability, equity) and explain the reasoning behind a recommended course of action.
criteria: Applies at least one named evaluation criterion and explains what it reveals about the response being evaluated
Uses the criterion to justify a recommended course of action, not just to describe the options

width.minimum: Apply at least one named criterion (e.g. efficiency, equity) to evaluate a response to an economic issue and explain what the criterion reveals about the response.
width.typical: Evaluate a response using criteria such as efficiency, profitability or equity to explain reasons for a course of action — for example, using economic performance indicators to identify variations within the Australian economy and evaluate government intervention responses.
wider: Apply multiple criteria to the same response and evaluate whether the criteria point to the same recommendation or require a trade-off decision
Investigate how equity and efficiency criteria can conflict in economic policy (e.g. progressive taxation) and evaluate how governments typically navigate the trade-off
Compare how different stakeholders (business, government, community) would weight the same set of evaluation criteria differently for the same decision

modes.reason: Apply criteria-based evaluation to different economic contexts — policy evaluation, business decision, consumer choice — so students can use criteria flexibly and not just in one context type.

nodes.label: Developing and justifying a response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a response to an economic or business issue and justify it using cost-benefit analysis and/or criteria-based evaluation, incorporating opportunity cost reasoning.
criteria: Produces a specific recommended course of action, not just a description of options
Provides at least two pieces of cost-benefit or criteria-based reasoning that justify the recommendation

width.minimum: Develop a recommended course of action for one economic issue and provide at least two pieces of cost-benefit or criteria-based reasoning to justify it.
width.typical: Develop and evaluate a response to an economic and business issue, using cost-benefit analysis or criteria to justify a recommended course of action; incorporate opportunity cost reasoning and address both short- and long-term implications.
wider: Develop a response to a real current economic policy issue (e.g. housing affordability, energy costs) and evaluate it against multiple criteria, acknowledging trade-offs
Present a justified response to a business decision scenario and explain how the recommendation would change under different economic conditions
Critically evaluate a published response to an economic issue (e.g. a policy proposal, a business strategy) using cost-benefit analysis and identify what the original evaluation missed or overstated

modes.reason: This node integrates CBA, opportunity cost, time-horizon analysis and criteria-based evaluation into a single justified recommendation. It is the descriptor's full demand — not just evaluating, but developing and justifying a response.

descriptors.title: Create referenced economic arguments
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge and research findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create descriptions, explanations and arguments using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S05). They have practised using discipline-specific vocabulary, presenting structured arguments and acknowledging sources. Y10 builds on this with more complex arguments, authoritative tone, and use of a broader vocabulary set across the full Year 10 topic scope.

nodes.label: Using economic vocabulary accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use economic and business terms accurately and contextually — selecting the right term for the right idea and using it in a way that demonstrates understanding.
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate vocabulary use is the baseline for credible economic communication. Students who use terms loosely or interchangeably (e.g. confusing 'fiscal' and 'monetary', or 'income' and 'wealth') undermine the authority of their arguments.
criteria: Uses at least five economic terms accurately, in context, without significant definitional errors
Selects terms appropriate to the specific topic (i.e. does not apply terms generically across all topics)

width.minimum: Use at least five economic or business terms accurately in an explanation of an economic issue, selecting terms that are appropriate to the specific topic.
width.typical: Use economic and business terms accurately in written and oral communication, including terms such as 'economic indicators', 'government intervention', 'fiscal policy', 'standard of living', 'economic performance', 'federal Budget', 'productivity', 'organisational structures', 'workforce management', 'superannuation', 'interdependence', 'trade', 'comparative advantage', 'globalisation', 'supply chain' and 'insurance'.
wider: Analyse how expert economic commentators (RBA Governor, Treasury Secretary) use technical vocabulary strategically to shape audience understanding and evaluate the communicative choices made
Compare how the same economic concept is described for specialist audiences (academic, policy) vs general audiences (news, social media) and evaluate what is gained and lost
Investigate how economic terminology has evolved — identifying terms that have changed meaning, been replaced or become contested — and evaluate implications for communication

modes.reason: Practise accurate term use across multiple topics — not just in one explanation. Repeated use in varied contexts builds precision. Peer feedback on vocabulary accuracy is particularly effective here.

nodes.label: Creating descriptions and explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create structured descriptions and explanations of economic issues that orient the audience to the issue and incorporate research findings with acknowledgement.
criteria: Produces an explanation that context-sets the issue before developing the explanation
Incorporates and acknowledges at least one research finding (with attribution)

width.minimum: Write a structured explanation of one economic issue that includes context-setting, key concepts with accurate vocabulary, and at least one acknowledged research finding.
width.typical: Create descriptions and explanations that orient the audience to the issue using relevant economic concepts and terms; incorporate and acknowledge research findings in appropriate formats such as reports and webpages; explain decisions and conclusions supported by reasons and data representations.
wider: Create an explanation for two different audiences (e.g. peers and business representatives) on the same economic issue and evaluate what changes and why
Write an explanation that incorporates visual data representation (table, chart) and explains how the visual supports the written argument
Investigate the conventions of economic reporting (executive summary, findings, evidence base) and produce an explanation that follows professional conventions

modes.reason: Apply explanation writing to varied economic topics and varied audiences — the skill transfers when students have practised it across contexts rather than perfected it for one.

nodes.label: Constructing economic arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct an argument for a course of action in response to an economic or business issue, applying an authoritative tone appropriate to purpose and audience.
criteria: Presents a clear claim for a course of action at the start of the argument
Supports the claim with at least one piece of evidence and one reason, and uses authoritative rather than tentative tone

width.minimum: Write one argument for a course of action on an economic issue, including at least one reason supported by evidence and an appropriate concluding recommendation.
width.typical: Present an argument for a proposal in response to an economic or business issue, applying authoritative tone appropriate to the purpose and audience (e.g. business manager, entrepreneur); support the argument with reasons and data representations; make and justify predictions about impacts.
wider: Construct a counter-argument to a position on an economic issue and evaluate which argument is stronger based on the evidence available
Write an economic policy argument for a government audience, applying the conventions of policy communication (problem statement, evidence base, recommended action, evaluation criteria)
Investigate how persuasive rhetoric and economic evidence interact in political economic communication and evaluate whether the argument is driven by evidence or framing

modes.reason: Apply argument construction to varied economic issues and varied audiences — the skill must generalise beyond practice in one context. Different topics require different evidence bases and different argumentative moves.
